chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Introductory
paragraphs: I dedicate this volume to the beloved and mourned memory of the woman who inspired, and partly wrote, all that is best in my writings--the friend and wife whose profound sense of truth and right gave me my strongest encouragement, and whose approval was my greatest reward. Like everything I have written for many years, this work belongs as much to her as to me. Yet in its present form it has received far too little of the priceless benefit of her revision: some of its most important passages were set aside for a more careful reconsideration that they will now never receive. If I could convey to the world even half the great thoughts and noble feelings buried in her grave, I would give it a greater benefit than anything I am ever likely to write without the prompting and help of her almost unequalled wisdom.

The grand, leading principle, towards which every argument unfolded in these pages directly converges, is the absolute and essential importance of human development in its richest diversity.--WILHELM VON HUMBOLDT: Sphere and Duties of Government.

The subject of this Essay is not what is called Liberty of the Will, so unfortunately set against the misleadingly named doctrine of Philosophical Necessity. It is Civil, or Social Liberty: the nature and limits of the power that society may legitimately exercise over an individual. This question is seldom formulated, and scarcely ever discussed, in general terms. Yet its unacknowledged presence deeply influences the practical disputes of our age, and it will probably soon be recognised as the vital question of the future. Far from being new, it has in a sense divided humanity from almost the earliest times. But at the stage of progress now reached by the more civilised parts of the human race, the question arises under new conditions and calls for a different and more fundamental examination.

The conflict between Liberty and Authority is the most prominent feature of the history we first become familiar with, especially that of Greece, Rome, and England. In earlier times, however, this was a conflict between subjects, or particular classes of subjects, and their government. Liberty meant protection against the tyranny of political rulers. Except in some of the popular governments of Greece, rulers were thought to occupy a position necessarily opposed to the people they governed. The ruler was a single governing person, or a governing tribe or caste, whose authority came from inheritance or conquest. In any event, they did not hold power at the will of the governed, and people did not dare, and perhaps did not wish, to challenge their supremacy, whatever precautions they took against its oppressive use. Their power was considered necessary, but also extremely dangerous: a weapon they would try to turn against their subjects as readily as against foreign enemies. To keep the weaker members of the community from becoming the prey of countless vultures, there had to be a beast of prey stronger than the others, charged with holding them in check. But the king of the vultures would be just as eager to feed upon the flock as any of the lesser harpies. The people therefore had to remain constantly on their guard against his beak and claws. Patriots accordingly sought to limit the power the ruler was permitted to exercise over the community; by liberty they meant this limitation. They pursued it in two ways. First, they sought recognition of certain immunities, called political liberties or rights. A ruler who violated these would be held to have broken his duty, and such a violation was considered to justify resistance to the particular act, or a general rebellion. The second method, usually adopted later, was to establish constitutional checks. These made some of the government's more important acts conditional on the consent of the community, or of some body assumed to represent its interests. In most European countries the ruling power was compelled to accept, to a greater or lesser extent, the first kind of limitation. This was not true of the second. To secure constitutional checks, or to extend them where they already existed in some measure, became everywhere the chief aim of those who loved liberty. And as long as people were content to fight one enemy by means of another, and to live under a master provided they had a more or less effective guarantee against his tyranny, their ambitions went no further.

In the course of human affairs, however, a time came when people no longer thought it a necessity of nature that their governors should be an independent power with interests opposed to their own. It seemed far better that the various magistrates of the State should be their tenants or delegates, whom they could dismiss whenever they chose. Only in this way, it appeared, could they be fully assured that governmental powers would never be abused to their disadvantage. Gradually, wherever a popular party existed, this new demand for elected rulers holding office temporarily became its principal aim. To a considerable extent, it displaced the earlier effort to restrict the rulers' power. As the struggle advanced to make authority derive from the periodic choice of the governed, some began to think that limiting the power itself had been given too much importance. Such limits, they might argue, were a safeguard against rulers whose interests were normally opposed to those of the people. What was needed now was for the rulers to identify with the people, so that their interests and will would be those of the nation. The nation needed no protection against its own will; there was no danger that it would tyrannise over itself. If the rulers were truly answerable to it, and could be promptly removed by it, the nation could safely entrust them with power whose use it could itself direct. Their power was simply the nation's own, concentrated into a form convenient for use. This way of thinking--or perhaps, more accurately, of feeling--was common in the last generation of European liberalism, and apparently still predominates in its Continental branch. Among the political thinkers of the Continent, those who acknowledge any limit to what a government may do stand out as brilliant exceptions, unless they are discussing governments which they believe ought not to exist at all. A similar feeling might by now have prevailed in our own country, had the circumstances which encouraged it for a time continued unchanged.

But success exposes weaknesses and faults in political and philosophical theories, as it does in people, that failure might have kept out of sight. When popular government existed only in dreams, or in accounts of some remote period of history, the idea that the people need not limit their power over themselves might have seemed self-evident. Nor did temporary aberrations such as those of the French Revolution necessarily shake this belief. The worst of them were committed by a small number who had seized power; and in any case they arose from a sudden, violent revolt against monarchical and aristocratic despotism, rather than from the continuing operation of popular institutions. In time, however, a democratic republic occupied a vast stretch of the earth and became one of the most powerful members of the community of nations. Government by elected representatives answerable to the people then became subject to the observation and criticism directed at a great established fact. People now saw that phrases such as "self-government," and "the power of the people over themselves," did not describe the situation accurately. The "people" exercising power are not always the people over whom it is exercised. And the "self-government" in question means that each person is governed by everyone else, rather than that each governs himself. In practice, moreover, the people's will means the will of their most numerous or most active section: the majority, or those who manage to get themselves accepted as the majority. The people may therefore wish to oppress some of their own number, and safeguards against this are as necessary as safeguards against any other abuse of power. Limiting governmental power over individuals thus remains just as important when those who hold power are regularly answerable to the community--which means, in practice, its strongest party. This understanding appealed equally to the intelligence of thinkers and to the inclinations of those important classes in European society whose real or supposed interests democracy threatens. It therefore established itself without difficulty; and political thinking now generally includes "the tyranny of the majority" among the evils against which society must be on its guard.

Like other forms of tyranny, the tyranny of the majority was at first feared mainly for what it could do through the public authorities; that is still the common view. Thoughtful people, however, saw that when society itself becomes the tyrant--the collective body ruling over the separate individuals who compose it--its instruments of tyranny extend beyond the acts of its political officials. Society can enforce its own commands, and does so. If it gives wrong commands instead of right ones, or gives any commands at all about matters in which it ought not to interfere, it exercises a social tyranny more formidable than many forms of political oppression. Although this tyranny does not usually impose such extreme penalties, it offers fewer means of escape: it reaches much further into the details of life and enslaves the soul itself. Protection against the tyranny of the magistrate is therefore insufficient. We also need protection against the tyranny of prevailing opinion and feeling; against society's tendency to impose its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on dissenters by means other than legal penalties; against its attempts to restrict the development, and if possible prevent the emergence, of any individuality at odds with its ways, and to force every character into its own mould. Collective opinion has a legitimate limit to its interference with individual independence. Finding that limit, and defending it against encroachment, is as essential to a sound state of human affairs as protection against political despotism.

Though few are likely to dispute this proposition in general terms, almost everything remains to be done about the practical question: where should the limit be set--how should individual independence and social control be properly balanced? Everything that makes life valuable to anyone depends on enforcing restraints on the actions of others. Some rules of conduct must therefore be imposed: first through law, and through opinion in many matters unsuitable for legal regulation. What these rules should be is the central question of human affairs. Yet, apart from a few of the most obvious cases, it is a question towards whose solution remarkably little progress has been made. No two ages, and scarcely any two countries, have answered it in the same way; the answer given by one age or country astonishes another. Nevertheless, the people of any particular age and country see no more difficulty in it than if humanity had always agreed on the subject. Their own established rules seem to them self-evident and in no need of justification. This almost universal illusion illustrates the magical power of custom. Custom is not merely a second nature, as the proverb says: it is continually mistaken for the first. Custom's power to prevent doubts about the rules of conduct people impose on one another is all the greater because this is a subject on which reasons are not generally thought necessary. People do not think they need to give reasons either to others or to themselves. They are used to believing--and some who aspire to be philosophers have encouraged the belief--that on matters of this kind their feelings are better than reasons and make reasons unnecessary. In practice, their opinions about regulating human conduct are guided by each person's feeling that everyone should be required to behave as he and those he sympathises with would like them to behave. Certainly no one admits to himself that his own liking is his standard of judgement. But an opinion about conduct unsupported by reasons can count only as one person's preference. If the reasons offered merely appeal to a similar preference in others, it is still a matter of liking, shared by many people instead of one. To an ordinary man, however, his own preference, backed in this way, is a wholly satisfactory reason. It is generally the only reason he has for any of his beliefs about morality, taste, or propriety that are not explicitly set out in his religious creed; and even in interpreting that creed, preference is his chief guide. People's opinions about what deserves praise or blame are consequently shaped by all the varied causes that affect their wishes about other people's behaviour. These causes are as numerous as those determining their wishes on any other subject. Sometimes it is their reason; at other times, their prejudices or superstitions; often their social affections, and not infrequently their anti-social ones--their envy or jealousy, their arrogance or contempt. Most often it is their desires or fears on their own behalf, their legitimate or illegitimate self-interest. Wherever one class is dominant, much of the country's morality springs from that class's interests and its sense of superiority. The morality governing relations between Spartans and Helots, between planters and negroes, between princes and subjects, between nobles and roturiers, and between men and women has largely been created by these class interests and feelings. The sentiments they produce in turn affect the moral feelings of members of the dominant class in their dealings with one another. Conversely, where a formerly dominant class has lost its position, or where its dominance is unpopular, prevailing moral sentiments often reflect an impatient resentment of superiority. Another major force determining the rules of conduct enforced by law or opinion--rules about what to do as well as what to refrain from doing--has been human servility towards the supposed likes and dislikes of worldly rulers or gods. Though essentially selfish, this servility is not hypocrisy. It produces entirely sincere feelings of abhorrence; it led people to burn magicians and heretics. Among these many baser influences, society's general and obvious interests have of course also played a part, and a large one, in directing moral sentiments. They have done so, however, less through reason and on their own merits than through the sympathies and antipathies they have generated. And sympathies and antipathies with little or no connection to society's interests have exerted just as powerful an influence in establishing moral codes.

The likes and dislikes of society, or of some powerful section of it, have thus been the chief practical influence determining the rules prescribed for everyone, under threat of legal penalties or public condemnation. Even those ahead of society in thought and feeling have generally left this state of affairs unchallenged in principle, however much they have opposed particular details of it. They have asked what society ought to like or dislike, rather than whether its likes and dislikes should have the force of law for individuals. They have preferred to try to change people's feelings on the particular points where they themselves were heretics, instead of joining heretics generally in a common defence of freedom. Religious belief is the only subject on which more than an isolated individual here and there has consistently taken the broader stand as a matter of principle. This case teaches us much, not least because it so strikingly illustrates the fallibility of what is called the moral sense: in a sincere bigot, odium theologicum is among the clearest examples of moral feeling. Those who first threw off the yoke of what called itself the Universal Church were generally as unwilling as that church to allow differences of religious opinion. But the heat of the conflict eventually passed without any party gaining a complete victory. Each church or sect had to restrict its hopes to keeping the ground it already held. Minorities, seeing no prospect of becoming majorities, were forced to plead for permission to differ from those they could not convert. It is therefore almost exclusively on this battlefield that the rights of individuals against society have been asserted on broad principles, and society's claim to authority over dissenters openly disputed. The great writers to whom the world owes the religious liberty it enjoys have mostly upheld freedom of conscience as an indefeasible right, absolutely denying that a human being is answerable to others for his religious belief. Yet people are so naturally intolerant about whatever they truly care for that religious freedom has scarcely anywhere become a practical reality unless religious indifference has also tipped the balance--the indifference that dislikes having its peace disturbed by theological quarrels. Almost all religious people, even in the most tolerant countries, admit the duty of toleration with unspoken reservations. One person accepts disagreement about church government but not about dogma; another can tolerate anyone except a Papist or a Unitarian; another tolerates everyone who believes in revealed religion. A few extend their charity a little further, but draw the line at belief in a God and in a future state. Wherever the majority's feeling remains sincere and intense, it has given up little of its claim to obedience.

The particular course of England's political history has made the burden of law lighter here than in most other European countries, although the burden of opinion may be heavier. There is considerable resistance to direct interference by the legislature or executive in private conduct. This comes less from a proper respect for individual independence than from the surviving habit of seeing the government as representing an interest opposed to the public's. The majority have not yet learnt to regard the government's power as their own power, or its opinions as their own opinions. When they do, individual liberty will probably be as vulnerable to government interference as it already is to public opinion. For now, however, strong feeling can still be aroused against attempts to use the law to control individuals in matters where they have not previously been accustomed to such control. This feeling makes very little distinction between matters that lie within the legitimate scope of law and those that do not. Consequently, although highly beneficial on the whole, it is perhaps as often misplaced as justified in the particular cases where it is applied. In fact, there is no recognised principle commonly used to judge whether governmental interference is proper or improper. People decide by personal preference. Some would gladly urge the government to take charge whenever they see something good to be done or an evil to be remedied. Others would rather endure almost any amount of social evil than add another area of human interests to those subject to governmental control. In a particular case, people take one side or the other according to this general tendency of their feelings, or according to how much they care about the particular action proposed for the government, or according to whether they believe it would carry out that action in the way they favour. Very rarely do they decide on the basis of a consistent view about which things a government is fit to undertake. It seems to me that this lack of a rule or principle leaves each side wrong about as often as the other: governmental interference is improperly demanded and improperly condemned with roughly equal frequency.

This Essay aims to establish one very simple principle as the absolute rule governing society's use of compulsion and control over individuals, whether through physical force in the form of legal penalties or through the moral coercion of public opinion. The principle is this: self-protection is the only purpose that justifies people, individually or collectively, in interfering with the freedom of action of any of their number. The only rightful reason to exercise power against the will of a member of a civilised community is to prevent harm to others. His own welfare, physical or moral, is not sufficient justification. He cannot rightfully be forced to act or refrain from acting because doing so would be better for him, would make him happier, or would, in other people's opinion, be wise or even right. Such considerations are good reasons to protest to him, reason with him, persuade him, or plead with him. They are not reasons to compel him, or to inflict any harm on him if he acts otherwise. To justify that, the conduct one seeks to prevent must be likely to harm someone else. A person is answerable to society only for the part of his conduct that concerns other people. In matters that concern himself alone, his independence is absolute as a matter of right. Over himself--over his own body and mind--the individual is sovereign.

It scarcely needs saying, perhaps, that this doctrine applies only to human beings whose faculties have reached maturity. We are not discussing children, or young people below the age that the law may set for manhood or womanhood. Those who still need others to care for them must be protected from their own actions as well as from injuries inflicted from outside. On the same grounds, we can leave aside those backward conditions of society in which the race itself may be regarded as still under age. The obstacles to spontaneous progress in its early stages are so great that there is seldom much choice about how to overcome them. A ruler animated by the desire for improvement is therefore justified in using any methods that will achieve an end perhaps otherwise unattainable. Despotism is a legitimate form of government when dealing with barbarians, provided that their improvement is its aim and that its methods are justified by actually achieving that aim. Liberty as a principle cannot apply before humanity has become capable of improvement through free and equal discussion. Until then, people have no alternative to unquestioning obedience to an Akbar or a Charlemagne, if they are fortunate enough to find one. But once people can be led towards their own improvement by conviction or persuasion--a stage long since reached by all the nations that concern us here--compulsion can no longer be admitted as a means of doing them good. Whether applied directly or through suffering and penalties for disobedience, it is justified only to protect others.

I should make clear that I give up any support my argument might draw from the idea of abstract right considered independently of utility. I take utility to be the final standard in every ethical question. But I mean utility in its widest sense, founded on the lasting interests of human beings as creatures capable of progress. Those interests, I maintain, justify bringing an individual's spontaneous action under external control only where his actions concern other people's interests. If someone does something harmful to others, there is a prima facie case for punishing him by law, or by general disapproval where legal penalties cannot safely be used. There are also many positive actions for others' benefit that he may rightfully be compelled to perform. These include giving evidence in a court of justice; contributing his fair share to the common defence, or to any other joint undertaking necessary to the interests of the society whose protection he enjoys; and performing certain acts of individual kindness, such as saving a fellow-creature's life or intervening to protect the defenceless from ill-treatment. Whenever such acts are clearly a man's duty, society may rightfully hold him responsible for failing to perform them. A person can harm others by inaction as well as by action, and in either case he is justly answerable to them for the injury. It is true that compulsion in the former case--inaction--must be exercised far more cautiously than in the case of harmful action. Holding someone responsible for harming others is the rule; holding him responsible for not preventing harm is, comparatively, the exception. Still, many cases are sufficiently clear and serious to justify that exception. In everything concerning his external relations, an individual is de jure answerable to those whose interests are involved and, if necessary, to society as their protector. There are often good reasons not to enforce that responsibility. But they must arise from the particular practical circumstances of the case: either the person is, on balance, likely to act better if left to his own judgement than under any control society could exercise, or the attempt at control would cause greater evils than it would prevent. When reasons of this kind rule out enforcing responsibility, the person's own conscience should occupy the empty judgement seat. It should protect the interests of others that have no outside protection, judging him all the more strictly because the circumstances do not allow him to be made answerable to the judgement of his fellow-creatures.

There is, however, an area of action in which society, as distinct from the individual, has at most an indirect interest. It includes all those parts of a person's life and conduct that affect only himself, or that affect others only with their free, voluntary, and undeceived consent and participation. By saying only himself, I mean directly and in the first instance. Whatever affects him may also affect others through him; the objection that might be based on this possibility will be considered later. This, then, is the proper domain of human liberty. First, it includes the inner life of consciousness. It requires liberty of conscience in the broadest sense: freedom of thought and feeling, and absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on every subject, whether practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. Freedom to express and publish opinions may seem to come under another principle, since it belongs to the part of an individual's conduct that concerns others. Yet it is almost as important as freedom of thought itself, and rests largely on the same grounds, so that in practice the two are inseparable. Secondly, the principle requires freedom of tastes and pursuits: freedom to plan our lives in accordance with our own characters, and to do as we please while accepting the consequences. Our fellow-creatures must not obstruct us so long as our actions do them no harm, even if they consider our conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong. Thirdly, each individual's liberty entails, within the same limits, freedom to combine with others. People must be free to join together for any purpose that does not harm others, provided that those joining are of full age and are neither forced nor deceived.

Whatever its form of government, a society is not free unless these liberties are generally respected; and it is not completely free unless they exist absolutely and without qualification. The only freedom worthy of the name is freedom to pursue our own good in our own way, provided we do not try to deprive others of theirs or obstruct their efforts to obtain it. Each person is the proper guardian of his own health, bodily, mental, and spiritual. Humanity gains more by allowing people to live as they themselves think best than by forcing each person to live as everyone else thinks best.

Though this doctrine is far from new, and may sound to some like a truism, none is more directly opposed to the general direction of current opinion and practice. Society has spent fully as much effort trying, according to its own understanding, to make people conform to its standards of personal excellence as to its standards of social excellence. The ancient commonwealths believed they were entitled to regulate every part of private conduct through public authority, and the ancient philosophers approved. Their ground was that the State had a profound interest in every citizen's entire bodily and mental discipline. Such a view might have been defensible in small republics surrounded by powerful enemies, constantly threatened with destruction by foreign attack or internal upheaval. Even a brief relaxation of energy and self-command could so readily have proved fatal to them that they could not afford to wait for freedom's beneficial long-term effects. In the modern world, political communities became larger. Above all, spiritual and temporal authority became separate, putting the guidance of people's consciences in different hands from the management of their worldly affairs. These changes prevented such extensive legal interference in the details of private life. But the instruments of moral repression have been used even more vigorously against departures from prevailing opinion in matters concerning oneself than in matters concerning society. Religion, the most powerful influence in forming moral feeling, has almost always been governed either by the ambitions of a hierarchy seeking control over every area of human conduct, or by the spirit of Puritanism. Nor have some modern reformers who most strongly oppose the religions of the past lagged behind churches or sects in asserting a right to spiritual domination. In particular, the social system M. Comte develops in his Traite de Politique Positive seeks to establish society's despotism over the individual--chiefly through moral rather than legal means--beyond anything envisaged in the political ideal of even the strictest disciplinarian among the ancient philosophers.

Beyond the particular doctrines of individual thinkers, the world at large shows a growing inclination to extend society's power over the individual too far, both through the pressure of opinion and through legislation itself. All the changes now taking place tend to strengthen society and weaken the individual. This encroachment is therefore not an evil likely to disappear of its own accord; on the contrary, it is likely to become increasingly formidable. Whether as rulers or as fellow-citizens, people are disposed to impose their own opinions and inclinations on others as rules of conduct. Some of the best feelings in human nature, as well as some of the worst, give this disposition such powerful support that almost nothing restrains it except a lack of power. And that power is growing, not declining. Unless a strong barrier of moral conviction can be raised against the harm, we must therefore expect it to increase in the world's present circumstances.

The argument will be easier to follow if, instead of beginning immediately with the general thesis, we first restrict ourselves to one branch of it where current opinion recognises the principle I have stated, at least to a certain extent, though not fully. That branch is Liberty of Thought, from which the related freedoms of speech and writing cannot be separated. To a considerable degree, these liberties form part of the political morality of every country that professes religious toleration and free institutions. Yet the philosophical and practical grounds on which they rest are perhaps less familiar to the public, and less thoroughly understood even by many leaders of opinion, than one might expect. Properly understood, those grounds apply much more widely than to a single division of the subject. A thorough examination of this part of the question will therefore provide the best introduction to the rest. I hope, then, that those who find nothing new in what I am about to say will excuse me for attempting one more discussion of a subject already discussed so often over the past three centuries.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion
paragraphs: We may hope that the time has passed when the "liberty of the press" needs defending as a safeguard against corrupt or tyrannical government. Surely no argument is now required against allowing a legislature or executive whose interests differ from the people's to dictate their opinions and decide which doctrines or arguments they may hear. Earlier writers have argued this aspect of the question so often and so decisively that it needs no special emphasis here. English press law remains as servile today as under the Tudors, but there is little danger of its actual enforcement against political discussion, except during a temporary panic when fear of insurrection makes ministers and judges abandon their usual restraint. Generally, in constitutional countries, we need not fear frequent governmental attempts to control the expression of opinion, whether the government is fully answerable to the people or not, except when it acts as the instrument of the public's general intolerance. Let us therefore assume a government wholly at one with the people, which never considers using coercive power unless it believes their voice supports it. I nevertheless deny the people's right to exercise such coercion, either directly or through their government. The power itself is illegitimate. The best government has no more right to it than the worst. Its exercise in agreement with public opinion is as harmful as, or more harmful than, its exercise against it. If everyone in the world except one person held one opinion, and that person alone held the opposite view, humanity would have no more justification for silencing him than he would have, if he possessed the power, for silencing humanity. If an opinion were a personal possession valuable only to its owner, and interference with its enjoyment merely a private injury, it would make some difference whether few or many suffered that injury. But suppressing an opinion has a special evil: it robs the human race, future generations as well as the present one, and those who disagree with the opinion even more than those who hold it. If the opinion is true, they lose the chance to exchange error for truth. If false, they lose a benefit almost as great: the clearer understanding and more vivid sense of truth that comes from its clash with error.

These two possibilities must be examined separately, since each corresponds to a distinct part of the argument. We can never know for certain that the opinion we are trying to suppress is false. And even if we could be certain, suppressing it would still be wrong.

First, an opinion that authority attempts to suppress may be true. Those seeking to suppress it naturally deny its truth, but they are fallible. They have no right to settle the question for all humanity and deprive everyone else of the means to judge it. Refusing to hear an opinion because they are certain it is false assumes that their certainty amounts to absolute certainty. Every attempt to silence discussion claims infallibility. This familiar argument is enough to condemn it; familiarity does not make the argument any weaker.

Unfortunately for human good sense, our fallibility carries far less weight in practical judgement than we always grant it in theory. Everyone knows perfectly well that he can be mistaken. Yet few think precautions against their own fallibility necessary, or allow that an opinion they feel entirely certain about might be an instance of the error to which they admit they are liable. Absolute rulers, and others accustomed to unquestioning deference, generally have this complete confidence in their opinions on almost every subject. More fortunate people, who sometimes hear their views challenged and have some experience of being corrected, place such limitless trust only in opinions shared by everyone around them or by those whose judgement they usually accept. For the less a person trusts his own unaided judgement, the more completely he generally trusts the infallibility of "the world" at large. But each person's world means the part he encounters: his party, sect, church, or social class. By comparison, a person may be called almost liberal and broad-minded if his world extends as far as his country or his age. Nor does knowing that other ages, countries, sects, churches, classes, and parties have believed, and still believe, the exact opposite shake his faith in this collective authority. He leaves his own world responsible for being right against other people's dissenting worlds. It never troubles him that chance alone determined which of these many worlds he trusts, and that the same influences making him a Churchman in London would have made him a Buddhist or a Confucian in Pekin. Yet nothing could be more evident, however much argument we add, than that ages are no more infallible than individuals. Every age has held many opinions that later ages judged not merely false but absurd. It is as certain that future ages will reject many opinions now generally accepted as that our own age rejects many once generally accepted.

The likely objection to this argument would run something like this. Forbidding the spread of error assumes infallibility no more than anything else public authority does on its own judgement and responsibility. People have judgement in order to use it. Should they be told never to use it because they may use it wrongly? Prohibiting what they consider harmful does not claim immunity from error; it fulfils their duty, despite their fallibility, to act on conscientious conviction. If we never acted on opinions because they might be wrong, we would neglect all our interests and leave every duty undone. An objection applying to all conduct cannot be a valid objection to any particular conduct. Governments and individuals must form the truest opinions they can, taking care in forming them and never imposing them on others without being completely sure they are right. Once sure, these objectors may say, refusing to act on those opinions is cowardice rather than conscientiousness. Why allow doctrines honestly believed dangerous to human welfare in this life or another to circulate unchecked merely because people in less enlightened times persecuted opinions now considered true? We should certainly avoid repeating that mistake. But governments and nations have also made mistakes in matters everyone accepts as proper subjects of authority: they have imposed bad taxes and fought unjust wars. Must we therefore impose no taxes and fight no wars, however great the provocation? People and governments must act as best they can. Absolute certainty does not exist, but sufficient assurance for the purposes of human life does. To guide our conduct, we may and must assume our opinion true. We assume no more when we prevent bad people from corrupting society by spreading opinions we consider false and harmful.

My answer is that we assume far more. There is an enormous difference between accepting an opinion as true because it has survived every opportunity for challenge, and assuming it true in order to forbid any attempt to refute it. Complete freedom to contradict and disprove our opinion is precisely what justifies treating it as true for purposes of action. On no other terms can a being with human faculties have rational confidence that he is right.

When we look at the history of opinion or the ordinary conduct of life, why are neither worse than they are? Certainly not because of the inherent power of human understanding. On any matter that is not self-evident, there are ninety-nine people wholly unable to judge for every one who can. Even the hundredth person's ability is only relative: most eminent people in every past generation held many opinions now known to be mistaken, and did or approved many things nobody would now defend. Why, then, do rational opinions and rational conduct generally predominate among people? If they really do--as they must unless human affairs are, and always have been, almost hopeless--the reason lies in one quality of the mind, the source of everything worthy of respect in human beings as intellectual or moral creatures: their errors can be corrected. People can put their mistakes right through discussion and experience. Experience alone is insufficient. Discussion is needed to show how experience should be interpreted. False opinions and harmful practices gradually give way to facts and arguments, but facts and arguments must be presented to the mind if they are to affect it. Very few facts speak for themselves without commentary bringing out their meaning. The entire strength and value of human judgement therefore rests on its ability to be corrected when wrong. We can trust it only while the means of correction remain constantly available. How has a person whose judgement genuinely deserves confidence acquired it? By keeping his mind open to criticism of his opinions and conduct. By making a habit of hearing everything that could be said against him, profiting from whatever was just, and explaining to himself, and sometimes to others, what was mistaken in the rest. By recognising that the only way a human being can approach a complete understanding of a subject is to hear people of every opinion discuss it, and study every way different kinds of mind can view it. No wise person has ever become wise otherwise, and human intelligence cannot become wise in any other way. Constantly correcting and completing one's opinions by comparing them with others' is not a source of doubt and hesitation in acting upon them. It is the only firm ground for justified confidence. Such a person knows everything that can, at least obviously, be said against him and has established his position against every challenger. He knows he sought objections and difficulties instead of avoiding them, and excluded no light that any quarter could throw on the subject. He is therefore entitled to consider his judgement better than that of any person, or any multitude, who has not undergone the same process.

We do not ask too much in requiring the public--that miscellaneous collection of a few wise and many foolish people--to accept the conditions that the wisest people, those most entitled to trust their judgement, find necessary before relying on it. Even the most intolerant church, the Roman Catholic Church, when considering a saint's canonisation, admits and patiently hears a "devil's advocate." Apparently, even the holiest person cannot receive honours after death until everything the devil could say against him has been heard and weighed. If questioning the Newtonian philosophy were forbidden, people could not feel as fully assured of its truth as they now do. Even our best-founded beliefs have no safeguard except a permanent invitation to everyone to prove them groundless. If nobody takes up the challenge, or if someone does and fails, we remain far from certainty. But we have done everything the current state of human reason allows. We have neglected nothing that could give truth a chance to reach us. As long as the contest remains open, we can hope that a better truth, if there is one, will be discovered when the human mind can receive it. Meanwhile, we can trust that we have come as close to truth as our time permits. This is the degree of certainty a fallible being can reach, and the only way to reach it.

It is strange that people accept the arguments for free discussion yet object to their being "pushed to an extreme;" they fail to see that reasons inadequate for an extreme case are inadequate for any case. It is strange, too, that they imagine themselves free of any claim to infallibility when they allow discussion on everything possibly doubtful, but forbid questioning some particular principle or doctrine because it is certain--meaning that they are certain of its certainty. To declare a proposition certain while someone would deny its certainty if allowed, but is forbidden to do so, assumes that we and those agreeing with us are the judges of certainty, and judges who need not hear the other side.

Our age has been described as "destitute of faith, but terrified at scepticism". People feel certain less that their opinions are true than that they would not know how to manage without them. Accordingly, an opinion's claim to protection from public attack is based less on its truth than on its importance to society. Certain beliefs, it is said, are so useful, even indispensable, to well-being that governments must uphold them just as they must protect any other social interest. In so necessary a matter, so directly within their duty, something short of infallibility is said to justify, and even require, governments to act on their own judgement when humanity's general opinion confirms it. It is also often argued, and even more often thought, that only bad people would want to weaken these beneficial beliefs. Restraining bad people and forbidding what only they would wish to do therefore seems unobjectionable. This reasoning makes restrictions on discussion depend on doctrines' usefulness rather than their truth, and congratulates itself on escaping the claim to be an infallible judge of opinions. Those satisfied by it fail to see that they have merely moved the assumption of infallibility from one point to another. An opinion's usefulness is itself a matter of opinion, as debatable, as open to discussion, and as much in need of discussion as the opinion itself. Unless the condemned opinion can fully defend itself, deciding that it is harmful requires an infallible judge just as much as deciding that it is false. It is no answer to allow a heretic to defend his opinion's usefulness or harmlessness while forbidding him to defend its truth. Truth is part of usefulness. Can we decide whether a proposition ought to be believed without considering whether it is true? The best people, not bad people, hold that a belief contrary to truth cannot be genuinely useful. Can we forbid them to make this argument when they are blamed for denying a doctrine said to be useful but which they believe false? Supporters of accepted opinions never fail to exploit this argument themselves. They do not treat usefulness as wholly separable from truth. On the contrary, they call their doctrine "the truth," and it is above all for this reason that they consider knowledge or belief in it indispensable. Usefulness cannot be fairly discussed when so vital an argument is available to one side but forbidden to the other. In fact, where law or public feeling forbids disputing an opinion's truth, it is equally intolerant of denying its usefulness. At most, it permits some qualification of the belief's absolute necessity, or of the positive guilt involved in rejecting it.

To show more fully the harm of refusing opinions a hearing because our own judgement has condemned them, we should bring the discussion to a definite case. I deliberately choose the cases least favourable to my position, where the case against freedom of opinion is considered strongest both in truth and in usefulness. Suppose the beliefs under attack are belief in a God and a future state, or any generally accepted moral doctrine. Arguing on this ground gives an unfair opponent a great advantage. He will certainly ask--and many people with no wish to be unfair will silently ask--whether these are doctrines I consider insufficiently certain for legal protection. Is belief in a God an opinion about which, I maintain, certainty amounts to claiming infallibility? But I must point out that I do not call confidence in any doctrine, whatever it is, a claim to infallibility. I mean deciding the question for others while denying them a hearing of the opposing case. I condemn this claim no less strongly when it supports my deepest convictions. Someone may be utterly convinced that an opinion is false and harmful; indeed, he may consider it not merely harmful but, to use expressions I wholly reject, immoral and impious. Nevertheless, if on that private judgement, even supported by his country's or his contemporaries' public judgement, he prevents the opinion from being heard in its own defence, he claims infallibility. Calling an opinion immoral or impious does not make this claim less objectionable or less dangerous. On the contrary, these are the cases where it is most disastrous. They are precisely the occasions when one generation makes the dreadful mistakes that fill later generations with astonishment and horror. Here we find history's memorable examples of the law being used to destroy the best people and the noblest doctrines. It succeeded deplorably against the people, although some doctrines survived--only to be invoked, almost in mockery, to defend similar treatment of those who reject them or their accepted interpretation.

Humanity can scarcely be reminded too often of the man named Socrates and his memorable conflict with the legal authorities and public opinion of his time. He was born in an age and country rich in individual greatness. Those who knew both him and his age best have presented him to posterity as its most virtuous man. We know him as the foremost model of every later teacher of virtue, the source alike of Plato's lofty inspiration and Aristotle's judicious utilitarianism--"i maestri di color che sanno," the two great sources of ethical and all other philosophy. This acknowledged master of all the eminent thinkers since his time, whose fame still grows after more than two thousand years and almost outweighs all the other names that glorify his native city, was judicially condemned and executed by his countrymen for impiety and immorality. His impiety lay in denying the State's recognised gods; indeed, his accuser claimed, as the "Apologia" records, that he believed in no gods at all. His immorality consisted in being, through his doctrines and teaching, a "corruptor of youth." There is every reason to believe the tribunal sincerely found him guilty. It sentenced the man who had probably served humanity better than anyone yet born to die as a criminal.

Let us turn to the only other judicial injustice whose mention after Socrates' condemnation would not be an anticlimax: what happened on Calvary a little more than eighteen hundred years ago. The man whose life and conversation left witnesses with so profound an impression of moral greatness that eighteen subsequent centuries have honoured him as the Almighty in person was put to a shameful death--on what charge? Blasphemy. People did not merely fail to recognise their benefactor. They mistook him for his exact opposite, treating him as the monstrous example of impiety they themselves are now considered for their treatment of him. Our feelings about these dreadful events, especially the second, make us deeply unjust towards the unfortunate people responsible. To all appearances they were not bad people, not worse than ordinary people, but rather better. They possessed fully, or more than fully, their time's and nation's religious, moral, and patriotic feelings. They were exactly the sort who, in every age including ours, are likely to live respected and free from blame. The high-priest who tore his garments on hearing words that his country's entire outlook regarded as the blackest guilt was probably as sincere in his horror and indignation as most respectable, pious people are today in their professed moral and religious feelings. Most who now shudder at his conduct would have acted just as he did had they lived in his time and been born Jews. Orthodox Christians tempted to believe that the people who stoned the first martyrs to death must have been worse than themselves should remember that Saint Paul was one of those persecutors.

Let us add another example, the most striking of all if an error's significance is measured by the wisdom and virtue of the person making it. If anyone in power ever had reason to consider himself the best and most enlightened person of his time, it was the Emperor Marcus Aurelius. As absolute ruler of the entire civilised world, he maintained throughout his life not only spotless justice but also, less expected from his Stoical upbringing, the tenderest heart. His few alleged failings all arose from indulgence. His writings, the ancient mind's highest ethical achievement, differ scarcely at all, if at all, from Christ's most characteristic teachings. This man, a better Christian in everything except dogma than almost any professedly Christian sovereign since, persecuted Christianity. He stood at the height of humanity's previous achievements, with an open, unrestrained intellect and a character that independently embodied the Christian ideal in his moral writings. Yet he failed to see that Christianity would benefit rather than harm the world to which he felt so deep a duty. He knew existing society was in a deplorable condition. But he saw, or thought he saw, that belief in and reverence for the accepted divinities held it together and kept it from becoming worse. As humanity's ruler, he believed he must not let society disintegrate. He could not see how new bonds could reunite it if its existing bonds were broken. The new religion openly sought to dissolve those bonds. Unless adopting it was his duty, suppressing it therefore appeared to be his duty. Christian theology seemed neither true nor divinely inspired to him. He could not believe the strange account of a crucified God. Nor could he foresee that a system claiming to rest entirely on a foundation he found so unbelievable would become the renewing force it has, despite all qualifications, actually proved to be. Thus the gentlest and most kindly of philosophers and rulers authorised Christianity's persecution from a solemn sense of duty. To me this is among the most tragic facts in history. It is bitter to consider how different the world's Christianity might have been had the empire adopted the faith under Marcus Aurelius rather than Constantine. Yet it would be unjust to him and untrue to deny that every argument available for punishing anti-Christian teaching was available to Marcus Aurelius for punishing Christianity's spread. No Christian believes more firmly that Atheism is false and dissolves society than Marcus Aurelius believed these things of Christianity, though he might have seemed the living person most capable of appreciating it. Anyone approving punishment for spreading opinions should therefore refrain from claiming, jointly with the multitude, the infallibility that the great Antoninus claimed with such unhappy results--unless he flatters himself that he is wiser and better than Marcus Aurelius, more deeply learned in his age's wisdom, intellectually further above it, more earnest in seeking truth, or more single-minded in serving it once found.

Opponents of religious freedom know that no argument for punishing irreligious opinions can avoid justifying Marcus Antoninus. When pressed, they sometimes accept this consequence and agree with Dr. Johnson that Christianity's persecutors were right. Persecution, they say, is a trial that truth ought to undergo and always survives: legal penalties ultimately have no power against truth, though they sometimes usefully defeat harmful errors. This defence of religious intolerance is remarkable enough that we must not pass it over without examination.

A theory justifying persecution of truth on the ground that persecution cannot harm it is not intentionally hostile to the acceptance of new truths. But its treatment of the people to whom we owe those truths can hardly be called generous. Revealing something of profound importance that the world did not know, or proving it mistaken on a vital worldly or spiritual concern, is among the greatest services one human being can render others. In certain cases, such as those of the early Christians and the Reformers, Dr. Johnson's followers regard it as the most precious gift humanity could receive. Yet this theory treats martyrdom as the proper payment for those splendid benefits. Rewarding their authors with the treatment of the vilest criminals is, on this account, no grievous mistake or misfortune for humanity to mourn in sackcloth and ashes. It is the normal and justifiable order. According to the doctrine, someone proposing a new truth should stand like someone proposing a new law under the Locrians' legislation: with a noose around his neck, ready to be tightened at once unless the public assembly, after hearing his reasons, adopts the proposal there and then. We can hardly suppose that people defending this treatment of benefactors value the benefit highly. I believe this view is mostly confined to those who think new truths may once have been desirable, but that we have had enough now.

In fact, the saying that truth always defeats persecution is one of those agreeable falsehoods people repeat to one another until it becomes commonplace, although all experience contradicts it. History overflows with instances of persecution suppressing truth. Even where suppression is not permanent, it can set truth back centuries. Consider religious opinions alone: the Reformation arose at least twenty times before Luther and was crushed. Arnold of Brescia was crushed. So was Fra Dolcino. So was Savonarola. The Albigeois were crushed, as were the Vaudois, the Lollards, and the Hussites. Even after Luther's time, persecution succeeded wherever it was maintained. Protestantism was eradicated in Spain, Italy, Flanders, and the Austrian empire. It would very probably have been eradicated in England too if Queen Mary had lived or Queen Elizabeth had died. Persecution has always succeeded unless the heretics were too numerous and powerful to be effectively persecuted. No reasonable person can doubt that Christianity could have been eradicated in the Roman Empire. It spread and gained supremacy because persecution was intermittent and brief, with long intervals when its propagation was almost undisturbed. Believing that truth, merely by being true, has some inherent power denied to error to withstand the dungeon and the stake is idle sentimentality. People are no more zealous for truth than they often are for error. Sufficient legal penalties, or even social penalties, will generally stop either spreading. Truth's real advantage is different: a true opinion may be extinguished once, twice, or many times, but over the centuries people will generally rediscover it. Eventually, one reappearance meets favourable circumstances in which it escapes persecution long enough to become strong enough to withstand every later attempt at suppression.

It will be said that we no longer execute the people who introduce new opinions. Unlike our fathers who killed the prophets, we even build their sepulchres. We do indeed no longer execute heretics, and modern feeling would probably not tolerate penalties severe enough to eradicate even the most detested opinions. But we must not congratulate ourselves on being free even from the stain of legal persecution. The law still penalises opinions, or at least their expression. Such penalties are enforced often enough even now that their eventual revival in full force is far from incredible. At Cornwall's summer assizes in 1857, an unfortunate man, reportedly blameless in every relationship of life, received twenty-one months' imprisonment for speaking some offensive words about Christianity and writing them on a gate. Within a month of that time, on separate occasions at the Old Bailey, two men were rejected as jurors for honestly declaring that they held no theological belief. A judge and one of the counsel also grossly insulted one of them. A third man, a foreigner, was denied justice against a thief for the same reason. This denial followed the legal doctrine that nobody may testify in court without professing belief in a God--any god suffices--and in a future state. The doctrine effectively declares such people outlaws, deprived of the courts' protection. They may be robbed or assaulted with impunity if the only witnesses are themselves or people of similar opinions. Anyone else may also be robbed or assaulted with impunity if proof depends on such witnesses. The underlying assumption is that someone who disbelieves in a future state takes a worthless oath. Those accepting this proposition show great historical ignorance: in every age, a large proportion of infidels have been distinguished for integrity and honour. Nor could anyone maintain it who had the slightest idea how many of the world's most respected people, for both virtue and achievement, are known at least to their intimates as unbelievers. The rule also destroys its own foundation. On the pretence that atheists must lie, it admits every atheist willing to lie and rejects only those who face public disgrace by admitting a hated creed rather than making a false statement. So plainly absurd by its own professed purpose, the rule survives only as a mark of hatred and a relic of persecution. And it is a peculiar persecution: people qualify for it by clearly proving they do not deserve it. The rule and its implied theory insult believers almost as much as infidels. If someone who disbelieves in a future state necessarily lies, then believers are kept from lying, if they are kept from it at all, only by fear of hell. We will not insult the rule's authors and supporters by supposing they derived this conception of Christian virtue from their own consciences.

These are admittedly only scraps and remnants of persecution. They might seem to reveal less a desire to persecute than a common weakness of English minds: the absurd pleasure of asserting a bad principle when no longer bad enough to want it actually applied. Unfortunately, public feeling offers no assurance that the suspension of worse forms of legal persecution, lasting roughly a generation, will continue. In our age, attempts to revive old evils disturb the calm surface of routine as often as efforts to introduce new benefits. What people now boast of as a religious revival is always, in narrow and uneducated minds, at least equally a revival of bigotry. Where popular feeling contains the strong, enduring element of intolerance always present in this country's middle classes, little is needed to provoke active persecution of people they have never ceased to consider proper targets for it. For it is precisely people's opinions and feelings about those who reject beliefs they consider important that prevent this country from being a place of intellectual freedom. For a long time, legal penalties have done their greatest harm by strengthening social stigma. That stigma is the truly effective force. It works so powerfully that openly professing socially forbidden opinions is much rarer in England than admitting opinions risking judicial punishment is in many other countries. Except for those financially independent of others' goodwill, opinion on these matters works as effectively as law. People might as well be imprisoned as deprived of their livelihood. Those whose livelihood is secure, who seek no favours from the powerful, from groups, or from the public, risk only being disliked and spoken against if they openly profess any opinion. Bearing this should not require exceptional heroism. No appeal ad misericordiam is appropriate on their behalf. Yet although we now inflict less harm on dissenters than we once did, our treatment of them may still harm ourselves just as much. Socrates was executed, but Socratic philosophy rose like the sun and illuminated the entire intellectual heavens. Christians were thrown to lions, but the Christian church grew into a magnificent, spreading tree, towering over older, weaker growths and smothering them in its shade. Our purely social intolerance kills nobody and eradicates no opinions, but persuades people to conceal them or refrain from actively spreading them. In this country, heretical opinions show no perceptible gain in ground, or even any perceptible loss of it, from one decade to the next or from one generation to another. They never flare widely but smoulder within the small circles of thoughtful, studious people where they begin. They never illuminate humanity's general affairs with either a true or a misleading light. This preserves conditions some minds find highly satisfactory: no unpleasant business of fining or imprisoning anyone, all prevailing opinions outwardly undisturbed, yet no absolute ban on the use of reason by dissenters afflicted with the disease of thought. It is a convenient arrangement for peace in the intellectual world, keeping everything much as it already is. But the price of this intellectual pacification is the sacrifice of the human mind's entire moral courage. Many of the most active and enquiring minds find it advisable to hide the real principles and grounds of their convictions. Addressing the public, they try to fit as many of their own conclusions as possible to premises they have privately rejected. Such conditions cannot produce the open, fearless characters or the logical, consistent minds that once adorned intellectual life. They can produce only people who conform to commonplace thinking, or opportunistic servants of truth whose arguments on every great subject are designed for their audiences rather than being those that convinced themselves. Those escaping this choice do so by narrowing their thoughts and interests to matters discussable without entering the realm of principles: small practical concerns that would resolve themselves if human minds were strengthened and enlarged, and that cannot be effectively resolved until then. Meanwhile, the very thing that would strengthen and enlarge those minds--free and daring inquiry into the highest subjects--is abandoned.

Those who see no evil in this silence on the part of heretics should first consider its consequence: there can never be a fair and thorough discussion of the heretical opinions themselves. Those opinions that could not survive such discussion do not disappear, even if their spread is checked. But heretics' minds do not suffer most from forbidding inquiry unless it reaches orthodox conclusions. The greatest injury falls on non-heretics, whose entire intellectual development is restricted and whose reason is intimidated by fear of heresy. Who can calculate the world's loss from all the promising minds joined to timid characters, afraid to pursue a bold, vigorous, independent line of thought lest it lead somewhere that might be called irreligious or immoral? Among them we sometimes find a deeply conscientious person with a subtle, refined understanding, spending his life in sophistical arguments with an intellect he cannot silence. He exhausts his ingenuity trying to reconcile conscience and reason with orthodoxy, perhaps without ever succeeding. Nobody can become a great thinker without recognising that his first duty as a thinker is to follow his intellect wherever it leads. Truth benefits more even from the errors of someone who thinks independently after proper study and preparation than from the correct opinions of people who hold them only by refusing to think. But freedom of thought is not needed solely, or chiefly, to create great thinkers. It is equally, and even more, indispensable if ordinary people are to reach their possible intellectual stature. Great individual thinkers have existed, and may exist again, amid general intellectual slavery. An intellectually active people has never existed, and never will, in that atmosphere. Whenever a people has temporarily approached that condition, fear of unorthodox inquiry has been suspended for a time. Where an unspoken agreement forbids questioning principles, and discussion of humanity's greatest questions is considered closed, we cannot expect the generally high level of intellectual activity that distinguishes certain historical periods. A people's mind has never been stirred to its foundations, with even ordinary intellects raised towards the dignity of thinking beings, when controversy avoids subjects large and important enough to inspire enthusiasm. We saw such an awakening in Europe immediately after the Reformation. Another came in the intellectual movement of the later eighteenth century, although confined to the Continent and a more cultivated class. A third, briefer still, came in Germany's intellectual ferment during the Goethian and Fichtean period. These periods produced widely different opinions. Yet all three shared the breaking of authority's yoke. In each, an old intellectual despotism had been overthrown and a new one had not yet replaced it. The impulses from these three periods made Europe what it is. Every single improvement that has since taken place, whether in the human mind itself or in the institutions under which people live, can be traced distinctly to one or another of those three periods. For some time, appearances have suggested that all three impulses are nearly exhausted. We can expect no new beginning until we reclaim our intellectual freedom.

We now turn to the argument's second part. Setting aside the possibility that accepted opinions are false, let us assume they are true and consider the value of the way people hold them when their truth is not freely and openly examined. Someone strongly convinced of an opinion may be unwilling to admit it could be false. But he should still recognise that, however true it is, unless it is discussed fully, frequently, and fearlessly, people will hold it as dead dogma rather than living truth.

Some people, fortunately fewer than formerly, think unquestioning assent to what they consider true is enough, even if the believer knows none of the reasons for it and cannot defend it against the shallowest objections. Once they secure authoritative teaching of their creed, they naturally think allowing questions can do no good and some harm. Wherever they prevail, rejecting the accepted opinion wisely and thoughtfully becomes almost impossible, although rejecting it rashly and ignorantly remains possible. Discussion can seldom be excluded altogether, and once it enters, beliefs without a foundation in conviction tend to collapse before the slightest appearance of an argument. But leave that possibility aside. Suppose the true opinion remains in the mind as prejudice, a belief independent of argument and impervious to it. This is not how a rational being ought to hold truth. It is not knowledge of truth. A truth held in this way is merely one more superstition, accidentally attached to words that state something true.

If people's intellect and judgement ought to be cultivated--as Protestants, at least, agree--what better subjects for exercising those faculties than matters so important to them that holding opinions on them is considered necessary? If cultivating understanding means one thing above all, surely it means learning the grounds of one's own opinions. On subjects where believing correctly is of the highest importance, people should be able to defend whatever they believe against at least the usual objections. Someone may answer: "Let them be taught the grounds of their opinions. It does not follow that opinions must be merely parroted because they are never heard controverted. Persons who learn geometry do not simply commit the theorems to memory, but understand and learn likewise the demonstrations; and it would be absurd to say that they remain ignorant of the grounds of geometrical truths, because they never hear any one deny, and attempt to disprove them." Certainly. Such teaching is sufficient in mathematics, where nothing can be said for the wrong side. Mathematical evidence is distinctive because all the argument lies on one side. There are no objections and no replies to objections. But wherever opinions can differ, truth depends on weighing two conflicting sets of reasons. Even in natural philosophy, the same facts can always receive another explanation: a geocentric theory rather than a heliocentric one, phlogiston rather than oxygen. We must establish why that alternative theory cannot be true. Until this is done, and until we understand how it is done, we do not understand our opinion's foundations. In the infinitely more complicated fields of morality, religion, politics, social relations, and practical life, three-quarters of the case for every disputed opinion consists in explaining away appearances favouring another view. Antiquity's greatest orator but one recorded that he always studied his opponent's case as intensely as his own, if not more intensely. Anyone studying a subject to find truth must imitate what Cicero did to succeed in court. Someone who knows only his own side knows little even of that. His reasons may be sound and remain unrefuted. But if he cannot refute the opposing reasons, or does not even know them, he has no basis for preferring either opinion. Rationally, he should suspend judgement. Unless content to do so, he either follows authority or, like most people, chooses the side that attracts him most. Nor is it enough to hear opponents' arguments from his own teachers, in their formulation and accompanied by their proposed refutations. That neither does the arguments justice nor brings them into real contact with his mind. He must hear them from people who actually believe them, defend them earnestly, and give them their strongest support. He must encounter them in their most plausible and persuasive form, and feel the full force of the difficulty the true view must confront and resolve. Otherwise he will never truly grasp the part of truth that answers that difficulty. Ninety-nine out of a hundred supposedly educated people are in this position, even among those who argue fluently for their views. Their conclusion may be true, but for all they know it could be false. They have never entered the standpoint of people who disagree or considered what those people might say. Consequently, in any proper sense of the word, they do not know the very doctrine that they themselves publicly profess to believe. They do not know the parts that explain and justify the rest: the considerations showing how apparently conflicting facts can be reconciled, or why one of two apparently strong reasons should prevail. They are strangers to the part of truth that tips the balance and determines a fully informed mind's judgement. Only those who have considered both sides equally and impartially, trying to see each side's reasons at their strongest, really know it. This discipline is so essential to understanding moral and human questions that, if important truths have no opponents, we must invent them and equip them with the strongest arguments the most skilful devil's advocate can devise.

An opponent of free discussion might try to weaken these considerations by saying that ordinary people need not know and understand everything philosophers and theologians can argue for or against their beliefs. There is no need for ordinary people themselves to be able to expose every misstatement or fallacious argument that an ingenious opponent may bring against them. It is enough that someone can answer, leaving nothing likely to mislead the uninstructed unrefuted. Simple minds can learn the obvious grounds of the truths taught to them and trust authority for the rest. Knowing they lack the knowledge and ability to resolve every possible difficulty, they can rest assured that all difficulties actually raised have been answered, or can be answered, by people specially trained for that purpose.

Let us grant this view everything claimed by those most easily satisfied with how little understanding need accompany belief in truth. Even then, the case for free discussion loses none of its force. This doctrine itself admits that people need rational assurance that every objection has been satisfactorily answered. But how can an objection be answered unless it is voiced? How can we know an answer is satisfactory unless objectors can show where it fails? If not the public, then at least the philosophers and theologians charged with resolving difficulties must know those difficulties in their most challenging form. That requires freedom to state them and present them in their strongest possible light. The Catholic Church has its own solution to this troublesome problem. It draws a sharp distinction between those permitted to accept its doctrines from conviction and those required to take them on trust. Neither group, admittedly, may choose what to accept. But clergy, at least those fully trusted, may properly and commendably study opponents' arguments in order to answer them, and may therefore read heretical books. Laypeople may do so only with special permission, difficult to obtain. This discipline recognises the value of knowing the enemy's case for teachers, while consistently finding ways to deny that knowledge to everyone else. It gives the elite greater intellectual cultivation, though no greater intellectual freedom, than the masses. It thereby obtains the kind of mental superiority its purposes need. Cultivation without freedom never produced a broad, liberal mind, but it can produce a clever nisi prius advocate for a cause. Countries professing Protestantism cannot use this expedient. Protestants maintain, at least in theory, that each person must bear responsibility for choosing a religion and cannot pass it to teachers. Moreover, in the world as it now stands, it is practically impossible to keep writings read by educated people out of uneducated people's hands. If humanity's teachers are to know everything they ought to know, everything must be free to be written and published without restriction.

Suppose that, where accepted opinions are true, lack of free discussion did no more harm than leave people ignorant of their grounds. We might then regard this as an intellectual rather than a moral evil, without effect on the opinions' value as influences on character. In fact, however, without discussion people forget not only an opinion's foundations but too often its meaning as well. Its words cease to call up ideas, or suggest only a fraction of the ideas they originally conveyed. A few memorised phrases replace vivid understanding and living belief. If meaning survives at all, only its outer shell remains; the finer substance is lost. This fact fills a great chapter in human history, one we cannot study or reflect on too seriously.

Almost every ethical doctrine and religious creed illustrates this experience. For their founders and the founders' immediate disciples, they are full of meaning and life. Their meaning remains just as strongly felt, and may become even more fully conscious, throughout the struggle to give the doctrine or creed supremacy over others. Eventually it either wins and becomes the generally accepted opinion, or stops advancing, holding the ground already gained without spreading further. Once either result becomes clear, controversy weakens and gradually dies away. The doctrine has become either an accepted opinion or one of the recognised sects or schools. Its believers have generally inherited rather than chosen it. Since conversion between such doctrines is now exceptional, it occupies little of their followers' attention. At first they were constantly alert, either defending themselves against the world or trying to win it over. Now they settle into acceptance, avoiding arguments against their creed whenever possible and no longer troubling dissenters, if any remain, with arguments for it.
