From this point in the history of a doctrine we can usually date the beginning of its decline in living power over those who profess it. Teachers of every creed often lament how difficult it is to keep believers vividly aware of the truth they nominally acknowledge, so that it enters their feelings and actually governs conduct. Nobody complains of this while a creed is still fighting for survival. Even its weaker champions then know and feel what they are fighting for and how it differs from other doctrines. During that stage, every creed has many adherents who have grasped its basic principles in every form of thought, weighed them in all their important connections, and experienced the full effect on character that belief ought to produce in a mind thoroughly imbued with it. But once a creed is inherited and passively rather than actively received, the mind no longer has to exercise its living powers so fully on the questions its belief presents. People increasingly forget everything except the formulas or give them a dull, sluggish assent. They act as though taking the belief on trust removed the need to realise it consciously or test it in personal experience. Eventually it almost loses contact with a human being's inner life. Then come the cases now so frequent that they nearly constitute the majority: the creed remains outside the mind like a hardening, petrifying crust, resisting every other influence directed at our higher nature. It shows its power by excluding fresh, living convictions, while doing nothing itself for mind or heart except guarding them to keep them empty.

The way most believers hold Christianity shows how doctrines capable of the deepest impression can remain dead beliefs, never becoming real to imagination, feeling, or understanding. By Christianity I mean here what every church and sect recognises as such: the maxims and precepts of the New Testament. All professing Christians regard them as sacred and accept them as laws. Yet it is hardly an exaggeration to say that fewer than one Christian in a thousand guides or tests his personal conduct by those laws. His actual standard is the custom of his nation, class, or religious body. On one side he has ethical maxims he believes infallible wisdom has given him to govern his life. On the other he has everyday judgements and practices that follow some maxims partway, others less far, and directly contradict others. Together they form a compromise between Christian belief and worldly interests and suggestions. He honours the first standard but truly obeys the second. All Christians believe that the blessed are the poor and humble, and those who are ill-used by the world; that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven; that they should judge not, lest they be judged; that they should swear not at all; that they should love their neighbour as themselves; that if one take their cloak, they should give him their coat also; that they should take no thought for the morrow; that if they would be perfect, they should sell all that they have and give it to the poor. They speak sincerely when they say they believe these things. They believe them as people believe what they have always heard praised and never heard debated. But as living beliefs governing conduct, they accept them only as far as customary practice goes. The complete doctrines are useful missiles against opponents, and people understand that, whenever possible, they should be offered as reasons for actions considered praiseworthy. Yet anyone pointing out that these maxims require countless things believers never contemplate doing would merely be classed with those deeply unpopular people who pretend to be better than everyone else. The doctrines have no real grip on ordinary believers, no power within their minds. People habitually respect their sound, but no feeling passes from the words to their meaning and compels the mind to grasp the realities and bring them into agreement with the formula. Whenever action is involved, they look to Mr. A and B to tell them how far to obey Christ.

We can be sure things were very different among the early Christians. Had they been otherwise, Christianity would never have grown from an obscure sect among the despised Hebrews into the Roman empire's religion. When their enemies said, "See how these Christians love one another"--something nobody is likely to say now--Christians surely felt their creed's meaning far more vividly than at any time since. This probably explains above all why Christianity now does so little to extend its territory, and after eighteen centuries remains almost confined to Europeans and their descendants. Even among the strictly religious, who take their doctrines very seriously and give many of them more meaning than most people do, the comparatively active part of their belief usually comes from Calvin, Knox, or someone else much closer to themselves in character. Christ's sayings remain passively alongside these beliefs, having scarcely more effect than the sound of such kind and gentle words itself produces. There are undoubtedly many reasons why doctrines distinctive to a sect stay more alive than those shared by all recognised sects, and why teachers work harder to preserve their meaning. But one reason is certainly that distinctive doctrines are challenged more often and must more frequently be defended against open opponents. Teachers and pupils alike fall asleep at their posts as soon as the enemy leaves the field.

Generally, the same is true of every inherited doctrine, whether concerned with prudence and knowledge of life or with morals and religion. Every language and literature abounds in general observations about what life is and how to behave in it. Everyone knows them, repeats them, or hears them with agreement. They are accepted as truisms, yet most people first understand their real meaning only when experience, usually painful, makes it real for them. How often does someone suffering an unexpected misfortune or disappointment recall a proverb or familiar saying known all his life, whose meaning, had he previously felt it as he does now, would have spared him the disaster? There are reasons besides lack of discussion for this. Many truths cannot be fully understood until personal experience brings them home. But even these truths would have yielded far more meaning, and that meaning would have struck far deeper, if the person had habitually heard people who understood them argue both sides. Half of humanity's errors arise from its disastrous tendency to stop thinking about a matter once it is no longer doubtful. A contemporary writer aptly calls this "the deep slumber of a decided opinion."

But what! someone may ask. Must disagreement exist for true knowledge to be possible? Must some people remain mistaken so that others can grasp the truth? Does a belief lose its life and reality the moment it becomes generally accepted? Can a proposition never be fully understood and felt unless some doubt remains? When everyone agrees on a truth, does that truth die within them? We have always thought the highest aim and best result of greater intelligence was to unite people increasingly in recognising every important truth. Does intelligence, then, survive only while it has not achieved its goal? Does the completeness of victory itself destroy the fruits of conquest?

I claim nothing of the kind. As humanity improves, the number of doctrines no longer disputed or doubted will steadily grow. Human well-being can almost be measured by the number and importance of truths that have become uncontested. The ending of serious controversy on one question after another is a necessary consequence of opinion becoming settled. Such settlement is as beneficial when opinions are true as it is dangerous and harmful when they are false. But although this gradual contraction of the range of disagreement is necessary in both senses--inevitable and indispensable--we need not conclude that every consequence is beneficial. Having to explain a truth to opponents or defend it against them greatly helps people understand it intelligently and vividly. Losing this aid is a considerable drawback to universal acceptance, though not enough to outweigh its benefit. Where opposition can no longer provide this advantage, I would like humanity's teachers to try to supply a substitute. They should devise some way to make learners as conscious of a question's difficulties as if an eager champion of the opposite view were pressing those difficulties upon them in an effort to convert them.

Instead of devising methods for this purpose, however, they have lost methods they once possessed. Socratic dialectics, magnificently illustrated in Plato's dialogues, provided one such method. These were essentially critical discussions of the great questions of philosophy and life. With consummate skill they showed someone who had merely absorbed the commonplaces of accepted opinion that he did not understand the subject, and had not yet given a definite meaning to the doctrines he professed. Recognising his ignorance would set him on the path towards a stable belief, grounded in a clear understanding of both the doctrines' meaning and the evidence for them. The school disputations of the middle ages pursued a somewhat similar aim. They sought to ensure that pupils understood their own opinion and, necessarily, its opposite, could support the grounds of one and refute those of the other. These contests had the incurable defect of deriving their premises from authority rather than reason. As intellectual training they were inferior in every respect to the powerful dialectics that formed the minds of the "Socratici viri". Nevertheless, the modern mind owes both far more than it generally admits. Today's educational methods contain nothing that remotely replaces either. Someone who learns everything from teachers or books may escape the constant temptation to be satisfied with cramming, but is still under no obligation to hear both sides. Consequently, knowing both sides remains uncommon even among thinkers. The weakest part of almost everyone's defence of an opinion is the intended answer to opponents. It is now fashionable to disparage negative logic: criticism that reveals weaknesses in theory or mistakes in practice without establishing positive truths. As a final result this would indeed be poor enough. But as a means to positive knowledge or conviction worthy of those names, its value cannot be overstated. Until people are systematically trained in it again, there will be few great thinkers and a low general level of intellect outside mathematical and physical inquiry. In other subjects, opinions deserve to be called knowledge only insofar as their holders have undergone, either through others' insistence or their own efforts, the same mental process demanded by active controversy with opponents. How much worse than absurd, then, to reject something freely offered that is so indispensable, yet so difficult to create when absent! If people challenge an accepted opinion, or would do so if law and public feeling permitted, let us thank them, open our minds to hear them, and rejoice. They perform for us a task we would otherwise have to perform ourselves with far greater effort, if we cared about either the certainty or the living force of our convictions.

One major reason for the value of different opinions remains to be discussed. It will retain its force until humanity reaches an intellectual stage that now seems immeasurably distant. So far we have considered two possibilities: the accepted view may be false and another therefore true; or the accepted view may be true but require conflict with the opposing error if its truth is to be clearly understood and deeply felt. More common than either is a third case. Conflicting doctrines share the truth, rather than one being true and the other false. The dissenting view is needed to supply the portion missing from the accepted doctrine. On subjects not directly evident to the senses, popular opinions are often true but seldom, if ever, contain the whole truth. They contain a part, sometimes larger and sometimes smaller, exaggerated, distorted, and detached from the other truths that should accompany and qualify it. Heretical opinions generally embody some of these suppressed or neglected truths, breaking the restraints that held them down. They either seek reconciliation with the truth in the common opinion or confront it as enemies, claiming with equal exclusiveness to be the whole truth themselves. So far, the latter has been more frequent: narrowness has always been the rule in human thought, breadth the exception. Thus, even in revolutions of opinion, one part of truth usually sets as another rises. Even progress, which should add to what we know, mostly substitutes one partial, incomplete truth for another. The improvement consists chiefly in the new fragment being more needed and better suited to the time than the fragment it displaces. Since prevailing opinions are partial even when founded on truth, every opinion containing some truth they omit should be treasured, however much error or confusion accompanies it. No sober observer of human affairs need be indignant because people who force overlooked truths upon our attention overlook truths we already see. Rather, while popular truth remains one-sided, unpopular truth may usefully have one-sided champions too. Such champions are generally the most energetic, and the most likely to force unwilling attention towards the fragment of wisdom they proclaim as the whole.

Consider the eighteenth century. Nearly everyone educated, together with the uneducated people they guided, was absorbed in admiration of what is called civilisation and the wonders of modern science, literature, and philosophy. They greatly exaggerated the differences between modern and ancient people, and believed every difference favoured themselves. Into this solid mass of one-sided opinion, Rousseau's paradoxes exploded like bombs, delivering a beneficial shock. They broke it apart and forced its elements to recombine in a better form, with new elements added. This does not mean prevailing opinions were generally further from truth than Rousseau's. They were closer, containing more positive truth and far less error. Yet Rousseau's doctrine contained a substantial amount of precisely the truth popular opinion lacked. Those truths travelled with it down the stream of opinion and remained as a deposit after the flood receded. Since Rousseau wrote, cultivated minds have never entirely lost the ideas that simplicity of life is superior, and that artificial society's constraints and hypocrisies weaken and demoralise people. In time these ideas will have their proper effect. For now, however, they need asserting as much as ever, and asserting through action, since words on this subject have almost exhausted their power.

In politics, too, it is nearly a commonplace that healthy political life needs both a party of order or stability and a party of progress or reform. It will need both until one expands its understanding enough to serve order and progress equally, distinguishing what deserves preservation from what should be swept away. Each outlook is useful because of the other's shortcomings. Yet it is largely their mutual opposition that keeps both reasonable and sane. Views favouring democracy and aristocracy, property and equality, co-operation and competition, luxury and abstinence, sociality and individuality, liberty and discipline, and every other enduring opposition in practical life must be expressed with equal freedom and advocated and defended with equal skill and energy. Otherwise neither element has a fair chance of receiving its due: one side of the scales will inevitably rise while the other falls. In life's great practical concerns, truth depends so much on reconciling and combining opposites that very few minds are broad and impartial enough to strike an approximately correct balance. It must therefore be reached through the rough process of combat between people fighting under hostile banners. On any of these great unsettled questions, if one opinion deserves not merely tolerance but encouragement and support more than the other, it is whichever happens to be in the minority at that time and place. For the moment, that opinion represents neglected interests, the aspect of human well-being at risk of receiving less than its share. I know that in this country differences of opinion on most of these subjects meet no intolerance. I offer these numerous, generally acknowledged examples to show a universal fact: given the present condition of human intelligence, only diversity of opinion offers a chance of fairness to every side of truth. Whenever some people depart from the world's apparent unanimity on a subject, even if the world is right, the dissenters probably have something worth hearing in their defence. Their silence would cost truth something.

Someone may object, "But some received principles, especially on the highest and most vital subjects, are more than half-truths. The Christian morality, for instance, is the whole truth on that subject, and if any one teaches a morality which varies from it, he is wholly in error." Since this is the most important practical case, none could better test the general principle. Before judging what Christian morality is or is not, however, we should decide what the expression means. If it means New Testament morality, I wonder how anyone who learns it from that book itself can suppose it was proclaimed or intended as a complete moral doctrine. The Gospel always refers to an existing morality. Its precepts address only those points where that morality needs correction or replacement by something broader and higher. Moreover, its language is extremely general, often impossible to interpret literally, and has the force of poetry or eloquence rather than the precision of legislation. Extracting a complete ethical system from it requires additions from the Old Testament: an elaborate system, certainly, but in many respects barbarous and intended only for a barbarous people. St. Paul explicitly opposed this Judaical way of interpreting his Master's doctrine and completing its scheme. He too, however, assumes an existing morality, that of the Greeks and Romans, and much of his advice to Christians accommodates them to it, even apparently sanctioning slavery. What is called Christian morality, and should more accurately be called theological morality, was not created by Christ or the Apostles. It arose much later, gradually constructed by the Catholic church during the first five centuries. Modern people and Protestants did not adopt it unquestioningly, but changed it far less than might have been expected. Mostly they removed additions made in the middle ages, each sect replacing them with fresh additions suited to its own character and tendencies. I would be the last to deny humanity's great debt to this morality and its early teachers. Nevertheless, I have no hesitation in calling it incomplete and one-sided on many important points. Without the contribution of ideas and feelings it did not sanction to European life and character, human affairs would be worse than they are. So-called Christian morality bears every mark of a reaction, largely a protest against Paganism. Its ideal is negative rather than positive, passive rather than active, Innocence rather than Nobleness, Abstinence from Evil rather than energetic Pursuit of Good. As has aptly been said, its precepts give "thou shalt not" too much precedence over "thou shalt." Horrified by sensuality, it idolised asceticism, an idol gradually reduced through compromise to one of legal observance. It offers hope of heaven and fear of hell as the designated, proper motives for virtue. Here it falls far below the best ancient thinkers, doing its utmost to make human morality essentially selfish by separating people's feelings of duty from their fellow-creatures' interests, except where self-interest gives them a reason to consider those interests. Essentially, it teaches passive obedience and submission to every established authority. Authorities must not be actively obeyed when they command what religion forbids, but however greatly they wrong us, they must not be resisted, much less rebelled against. In the best Pagan nations, duty to the State occupied even an excessive place, infringing rightful individual liberty. Purely Christian ethics scarcely notices or acknowledges this great field of duty. The Koran, not the New Testament, contains the maxim: "A ruler who appoints any man to an office, when there is in his dominions another man better qualified for it, sins against God and against the State." Modern morality's limited recognition of public obligation comes from Greek and Roman sources rather than Christian ones. Similarly, whatever magnanimity, high-mindedness, personal dignity, and even honour exists in private morality comes from the purely human rather than religious part of our education. It could never have grown from an ethical standard that professes to recognise worth only in obedience.

I am as far as anyone from claiming that these defects must belong to every possible conception of Christian ethics, or that the many requirements of a complete morality absent from it cannot be reconciled with it. Still less would I imply this about Christ's own doctrines and precepts. I believe his sayings accomplish everything the evidence suggests they were intended to accomplish. They conflict with nothing a comprehensive morality requires. Everything excellent in ethics can be included within them without straining their language more than everyone who has tried to derive any practical rule of conduct from them has already done. This is entirely consistent, however, with believing that they contain, and were intended to contain, only part of the truth. Many essential elements of the highest morality were neither supplied nor intended to be supplied by the recorded sayings of Christianity's Founder. The Christian Church's ethical system built upon those sayings then discarded these elements altogether. Given this, I consider it a serious mistake to keep seeking in Christian doctrine the complete rule of guidance its author meant it to endorse and enforce, but only partly to supply. I also believe this narrow theory is becoming a grave practical evil, greatly reducing the value of the moral training and teaching that so many well-intentioned people are at last working to promote. I greatly fear the results of trying to shape minds and feelings on an exclusively religious model while rejecting what, for want of a better name, we may call secular standards. These formerly coexisted with and supplemented Christian ethics, absorbing some of its spirit and communicating some of their own. Discarding them will produce, and already is producing, a low, abject, servile character. However completely it submits to what it regards as the Supreme Will, such a character cannot rise to, or sympathise with, the idea of Supreme Goodness. To regenerate humanity morally, ethical systems not derivable from exclusively Christian sources must exist alongside Christian ethics. Christianity is no exception to the rule that, while the human mind remains imperfect, truth needs different opinions. Recognising moral truths absent from Christianity does not require ignoring the truths it contains. Such prejudice or oversight, whenever it occurs, is wholly harmful. But we cannot expect always to avoid it, and must regard it as the price of an immeasurable benefit. We must and should protest when a part of truth claims exclusively to be the whole. If reaction makes the protesters unjust in turn, their one-sidedness, like the other side's, is regrettable but must be tolerated. Christians who want infidels to treat Christianity fairly should themselves treat infidelity fairly. Truth gains nothing by overlooking a fact familiar to anyone with even an ordinary knowledge of literary history: much of the noblest and most valuable moral teaching comes not merely from people who did not know Christianity, but from people who knew and rejected it.

I do not claim that unlimited freedom to express every possible opinion would end the harms of religious or philosophical sectarianism. People of limited understanding who earnestly believe a truth will certainly proclaim it, teach it, and often act on it as though no other truth existed, or at least none capable of limiting or qualifying it. I accept that even the freest discussion cannot cure opinions' tendency to become sectarian. Discussion often intensifies and aggravates it: people reject a truth they should have recognised all the more violently because those they regard as opponents proclaim it. But the beneficial effect of clashing opinions falls on the calmer, less interested observer, rather than the passionate partisan. The great evil is not violent conflict between portions of truth, but the quiet suppression of half of it. Hope always remains when people must hear both sides. When they attend to only one, errors harden into prejudice, and truth itself loses its proper effect by being exaggerated into falsehood. Few mental abilities are rarer than the judicial power to judge a question intelligently between two sides when only one has an advocate before it. Truth therefore has a chance only insofar as every side of it, every opinion containing any fragment of it, has advocates--and advocates who can obtain a hearing.

We have now established four distinct grounds for freedom of opinion and of its expression as necessities for humanity's mental well-being, on which all its other well-being depends. Let us briefly restate those grounds.
First, an opinion forced into silence may, for all we can know with certainty, be true. Denying that possibility claims infallibility for ourselves.

Secondly, even a mistaken opinion that is silenced may contain some truth, and very often does. Since the accepted or prevailing view on any subject seldom, if ever, contains the whole truth, only a clash with opposing views gives the remaining truth a chance to emerge.

Thirdly, even if the accepted opinion is true and contains the whole truth, it must be open to vigorous, earnest challenge and actually undergo it. Otherwise most believers will hold it as prejudice, scarcely understanding or feeling its rational foundations. Fourthly, more than this, the doctrine's own meaning risks becoming lost or weakened, losing its living influence on character and conduct. Dogma becomes a mere formal profession, powerless to do good yet occupying the ground and obstructing the growth of real, heartfelt conviction founded on reason or personal experience.

Before leaving freedom of opinion, we should consider the view that all opinions may be freely expressed provided their expression is moderate and stays within the limits of fair discussion. Much could be said about the impossibility of locating these supposed limits. If the test is offence to those whose opinion is attacked, experience, I believe, shows that they are offended whenever the attack is effective and powerful. Any opponent who presses them hard and proves difficult to answer seems immoderate to them if he displays strong feeling about the subject. Important though this is in practice, it gives way to a more fundamental objection. The manner of asserting even a true opinion can undoubtedly be deeply objectionable and deserve severe condemnation. But the chief offences of this kind are generally impossible to prove conclusively unless someone accidentally gives himself away. The gravest are using sophistry, suppressing facts or arguments, misstating the case, and misrepresenting the opposing opinion. Yet all these things, even in their worst forms, are constantly done in complete good faith by people not considered ignorant or incompetent, and often not deserving that description in other respects. It is therefore seldom possible to label such misrepresentation morally blameworthy conscientiously and on adequate grounds. Still less could the law presume to intervene in this misconduct in argument. Condemnations of what is usually called immoderate discussion--abuse, sarcasm, personal attacks, and the like--would deserve more sympathy if anyone proposed forbidding those weapons equally to both sides. Instead, people want only to prevent their use against prevailing opinion. Against unpopular views they can be used without general disapproval, and will probably earn their user praise for honest zeal and righteous indignation. Yet these weapons do their greatest harm when turned against people comparatively unable to defend themselves. And the unfair advantage they offer an opinion accrues almost exclusively to accepted opinions. The worst such offence a controversialist can commit is to brand opponents as bad, immoral people. Holders of unpopular opinions are especially vulnerable to this slander. Generally few and uninfluential, they have few people besides themselves much concerned to see them treated justly. Those attacking an accepted opinion, by contrast, cannot use this weapon. It would endanger them, and even if it did not, it would only damage their cause. As a rule, opinions contrary to accepted beliefs gain a hearing only through carefully moderate language and the most scrupulous avoidance of needless offence. Even a slight departure from this almost always loses them ground. Meanwhile, unlimited abuse on behalf of prevailing opinion genuinely deters people both from professing contrary views and from listening to their advocates. Truth and justice therefore make restraining this use of abusive language far more important than restraining the other. If we had to choose, for example, there would be much greater need to discourage offensive attacks on infidelity than on religion. Clearly, however, neither law nor authority has any business restricting either. Opinion should judge each instance according to its particular circumstances, condemning anyone, on either side, whose advocacy shows dishonesty, malice, bigotry, or intolerance. It must not infer these faults simply from the side someone takes, even when that side opposes our own. It should honour anyone, whatever his beliefs, who is calm enough to see and honest enough to state what his opponents and their opinions really are. Such a person exaggerates nothing against them and conceals nothing that supports, or might be thought to support, them. This is the true morality of public discussion. Though often violated, it is, I am glad to believe, largely observed by many controversialists and conscientiously pursued by still more.

If this chapter's arguments have any validity, people should enjoy the fullest freedom to profess and discuss any doctrine as an ethical conviction, however immoral others consider it. It would therefore be irrelevant to examine here whether Tyrannicide deserves that description. I will say only that it has always been an open moral question. Whole nations, and some of the best and wisest individuals, have regarded a private citizen's killing of a criminal who has raised himself above the law and beyond legal punishment or control as an act of exalted virtue rather than a crime. Right or wrong, such an act belongs to civil war rather than assassination. For that reason, I consider incitement to it in a particular case potentially punishable, but only if an overt act follows and at least a probable link between incitement and act can be established. Even then, only the government attacked, exercising self-defence, can legitimately punish an attack on its own existence; a foreign government cannot do so.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Of Individuality, As One of the Elements of Well-Being
paragraphs: These, then, are the reasons why human beings must be free to form opinions and express them without restriction. And these are the damaging effects on their intellectual nature, and through it their moral nature, if that freedom is neither granted nor exercised in defiance of prohibition. We must now ask whether the same reasons also require people to be free to act on their opinions: to put them into practice in their lives without physical or moral obstruction from their fellow-men, provided they do so at their own risk. This final condition is, of course, essential. No one claims that actions should be as free as opinions. Indeed, even opinions lose their protection when the circumstances of their expression turn it into a direct incitement to a harmful act. The opinion that corn-dealers starve the poor, or that private property is robbery, should be left alone when it is simply circulated in the press. But it may rightly be punished if spoken to an excited mob gathered outside a corn-dealer's house, or passed around that same mob on a placard. Acts of any kind that harm others without justifiable cause may be restrained by people's disapproval and, when necessary, their active intervention; in the more serious cases, such restraint is an absolute necessity. Individual liberty must have this limit: a person must not make himself a nuisance to others. But if he leaves others undisturbed in matters concerning them, and follows his own inclinations and judgement only in matters concerning himself, the reasons for freedom of opinion also establish his right to put those opinions into practice, undisturbed and at his own expense. Human beings are fallible; most of their truths are only half-truths; agreement in opinion is undesirable unless it results from the fullest and freest comparison of opposing views; and diversity is a benefit, not an evil, until humanity becomes far more capable than it now is of recognising every side of the truth. These principles apply just as much to people's ways of acting as to their opinions. While humanity remains imperfect, different opinions are useful; so too are different experiments in living. Varieties of character should have free scope, provided they do not injure others, and different ways of life should have their worth tested in practice whenever someone chooses to try them. In matters that do not primarily concern others, individuality should, in short, express itself. If other people's traditions or customs, rather than a person's own character, determine his conduct, one of the principal ingredients of human happiness is missing--and the most important ingredient of individual and social progress.

The greatest difficulty in defending this principle is not a disagreement about the means to an accepted end. It is people's general indifference to the end itself. Suppose people felt that the free development of individuality was one of the chief essentials of well-being; that it stood alongside everything meant by civilisation, instruction, education, and culture, and was also a necessary part and condition of them all. There would then be no danger of undervaluing liberty, and no extraordinary difficulty in settling its boundaries with social control. The trouble is that ordinary ways of thinking scarcely recognise any intrinsic value in individual spontaneity, or any claim it has to consideration for its own sake. The majority are satisfied with human ways as they stand--for it is the majority who make them what they are--and cannot understand why those ways should not be good enough for everyone. Moreover, spontaneity has no place in the ideal of most moral and social reformers. They tend instead to view it suspiciously, as a troublesome and possibly rebellious obstacle to the universal acceptance of what they themselves judge best for humanity. Outside Germany, few people even understand the doctrine that Wilhelm von Humboldt, so distinguished both as a savant and as a politician, took as the theme of a treatise: that "the end of man, or that which is prescribed by the eternal or immutable dictates of reason, and not suggested by vague and transient desires, is the highest and most harmonious development of his powers to a complete and consistent whole;" and that, consequently, the aim "towards which every human being must ceaselessly direct his efforts, and on which especially those who design to influence their fellow-men must ever keep their eyes, is the individuality of power and development;" that this requires two things, "freedom, and a variety of situations;" and that their union produces "individual vigour and manifold diversity," which together make up "originality."

However unfamiliar people may be with a doctrine such as Von Humboldt's, and however surprising they may find this high valuation of individuality, the disagreement must surely be only one of degree. No one's ideal of good conduct requires people to do absolutely nothing except copy one another. No one would say that people ought to leave no trace of their own judgement or individual character on their way of life or the management of their affairs. Equally, it would be absurd to suggest that they should live as though the world had known nothing before their birth, and experience had done nothing to show that one way of living or acting is preferable to another. Everyone agrees that the young should be taught and trained to know and benefit from the established results of human experience. But once a human being's faculties have matured, it is his privilege and proper condition to interpret and use that experience for himself. He must determine which parts of recorded experience genuinely apply to his own circumstances and character. Other people's traditions and customs provide some evidence of what experience has taught them. As presumptive evidence, they deserve his respect. But first, their experience may be too limited, or they may have interpreted it wrongly. Secondly, even a correct interpretation of their experience may not suit him. Customs are shaped for customary circumstances and customary characters; his circumstances or character may be unusual. Thirdly, even if a custom is good in itself and suitable for him, following it merely because it is customary does not train or develop any of his distinctively human qualities. Perception, judgement, discriminating feeling, mental activity, and even moral preference come into use only when a person makes a choice. Someone who acts simply because it is the custom makes no choice. He gets no practice in either recognising or wanting what is best. Mental and moral powers, like muscles, improve only through use. Doing something merely because others do it exercises these powers no more than believing something merely because others believe it. If the grounds of an opinion do not convince a person's own reason, adopting it cannot strengthen that reason and will probably weaken it. Likewise, when the motives for an action do not accord with his own feelings and character--in matters where affection or other people's rights are not involved--acting on them helps make those feelings and that character passive and sluggish instead of active and energetic.

A person who lets the world, or his own section of it, choose his way of life needs no faculty beyond the ape's ability to imitate. A person who chooses it for himself uses all his faculties. He must observe in order to see, reason and judge in order to foresee, make an active effort to gather the material for a decision, use discrimination to decide, and then use firmness and self-control to keep to his considered choice. He needs and exercises these qualities in direct proportion to how much of his conduct he determines by his own judgement and feelings. Perhaps he could be led along a good path and kept out of danger without any of them. But how would his worth as a human being compare? It matters not only what people do, but what kind of people do it. Of all the things human effort can rightly seek to perfect and beautify, surely the most important is the human being himself. Suppose machines--automatons in human form--could build houses, grow corn, fight battles, try legal cases, and even erect churches and say prayers. To replace even the men and women now living in the more civilised parts of the world with these automatons would be a considerable loss, although those people are certainly only undernourished examples of what nature can and will produce. Human nature is no machine, built to a model and set to perform exactly its assigned task. It is a tree that must grow and develop in every direction, following the internal forces that make it a living thing.

Most people will probably agree that we should exercise our understanding, and that following custom intelligently--or even occasionally departing from it intelligently--is better than blind, merely mechanical conformity. To some extent, people admit that our understanding should be our own. They are less willing to admit that our desires and impulses should also be our own, or that having impulses of our own, especially strong ones, can be anything but a danger and a trap. Yet desires and impulses belong to a complete human being just as much as beliefs and restraints do. Strong impulses are dangerous only when improperly balanced: when one set of aims and inclinations grows powerful while others that ought to exist alongside them remain weak and inactive. People behave badly because their consciences are weak, not because their desires are strong. There is no natural link between strong impulses and a weak conscience; the natural connection runs the other way. To say that someone's desires and feelings are stronger and more varied than another's is simply to say that he has more of the raw material of human nature. He may therefore be capable of greater evil, but he is certainly capable of greater good. Strong impulses are another name for energy. Energy can be put to bad uses, but an energetic nature can always be made to yield more good than an idle, unfeeling one. Those with the greatest natural feeling are always those whose feelings, when cultivated, can become strongest. The same intense sensitivities that make personal impulses vivid and powerful also give rise to the most passionate love of virtue and the sternest self-control. Society fulfils its duty and protects its interests by cultivating these qualities, not by discarding the material of heroes because it does not know how to form them. We say that a person has a character when his desires and impulses are his own: when they express his own nature as his own cultivation has developed and modified it. Someone whose desires and impulses are not his own has no more character than a steam-engine. If his impulses are not only his own but strong, and governed by a strong will, his character is energetic. Anyone who thinks that individuality in desires and impulses should not be encouraged to develop must hold that society has no need of strong natures, gains nothing from having many people of substantial character, and ought not to desire a high general level of energy.

In some early conditions of society, these forces could, and did, develop far beyond society's ability to discipline and control them. There was a time when spontaneity and individuality were excessive, and the social principle struggled hard to contain them. The difficulty then was to persuade people of strong body or mind to obey any rule requiring them to restrain their impulses. To overcome it, law and discipline, like the Popes in their struggle against the Emperors, claimed authority over the whole person. They demanded control of his entire life in order to control his character, which society had found no other adequate means of restraining. But society has now thoroughly gained the upper hand over individuality. The danger to human nature is too little personal impulse and preference, rather than too much. Things have changed enormously since the passions of those made powerful by rank or personal gifts habitually rebelled against laws and regulations, and had to be tightly chained if anyone within their reach was to enjoy even a little security. Nowadays everyone, from the highest social class to the lowest, lives as though watched by a hostile censorship they dread. Even in matters concerning only themselves, as well as in those concerning others, individuals and families do not ask: what do I prefer? What would suit my character and disposition? What would give the best and highest in me a fair chance to grow and flourish? Instead they ask: what is suitable for my position? What do people of my rank and financial circumstances usually do? Or, worse still: what do people of a higher rank and greater means than mine usually do? I do not mean that they choose the customary over what suits their own inclinations. It never occurs to them to have an inclination for anything except the customary. The mind itself thus bows under the yoke. Even when seeking pleasure, people think first of conformity. They live in crowds, choosing only among things commonly done. Unusual tastes and eccentric behaviour are shunned as much as crimes, until, through never following their own nature, they have no nature left to follow. Their human capacities wither and starve. They become incapable of strong wishes or pleasures that arise from within, and generally possess no opinions or feelings of their own growth, properly belonging to themselves. Is this, or is it not, the condition we should desire for human nature?

According to the Calvinistic theory, it is. In that theory, humanity's one great offence is Self-will, and all the good human beings can achieve is contained in Obedience. There is no choice: you must act in this way and no other; "whatever is not a duty, is a sin." Since human nature is fundamentally corrupt, no one can be redeemed until that nature has been killed within him. For anyone who holds this view of life, crushing a human faculty, capacity, or sensitivity is no evil. A person needs only the capacity to surrender himself to God's will. If he employs any faculty for a purpose other than carrying out that supposed will more effectively, he would be better without it. Such is Calvinism's theory. Many who do not call themselves Calvinists accept a milder form of it. They soften it by interpreting God's alleged will less ascetically: they say that he intends people to satisfy some of their inclinations. Naturally, this must happen through obedience, rather than in whatever way people themselves prefer--that is, in a manner prescribed by authority and therefore, by the very conditions of the case, the same for everyone.

In some such unobtrusive form, there is now a strong tendency towards this narrow view of life and the cramped, rigid type of character it favours. Many people undoubtedly believe in all sincerity that human beings so restricted and stunted are what their Maker intended. In much the same way, many have thought trees far finer when lopped into pollards or trimmed into animal shapes than when left as nature made them. But if religion includes the belief that a good being made humanity, it is more consistent with that belief to suppose he gave us all our faculties to be cultivated and developed, rather than uprooted and destroyed. We should suppose he delights in every step his creatures take towards the ideal embodied in them, and in every increase in their capacity to understand, act, or enjoy. There is another ideal of human excellence besides the Calvinistic: a view that human nature was given to us for purposes beyond merely renouncing it. "Pagan self-assertion" contributes to human worth alongside "Christian self-denial." The Greek ideal of self-development combines with the Platonic and Christian ideal of self-government, but is not displaced by it. Being a John Knox may be better than being an Alcibiades, but being a Pericles is better than either. And if a Pericles lived among us today, he would lack none of the good qualities possessed by John Knox.

Human beings become noble and beautiful to contemplate by cultivating and bringing out what is individual in themselves, within the limits set by others' rights and interests, rather than by wearing it down into uniformity. Since actions share the character of those who perform them, the same process makes human life richer, more varied, and more inspiring. It gives greater nourishment to high thoughts and elevated feelings, and strengthens each individual's bond with humanity by making humanity infinitely more worth belonging to. As a person's individuality develops, he becomes more valuable to himself and so capable of being more valuable to others. His own existence has a greater fullness of life; and when there is more life in the individuals, there is more in the whole they form. We cannot dispense with the restraints needed to prevent stronger human natures from violating other people's rights. But even from the standpoint of human development, those restraints bring ample compensation. The opportunities for development someone loses by being prevented from satisfying his inclinations at others' expense are chiefly opportunities that would have obstructed other people's development. Even for the person restrained, there is a full equivalent in the greater development of the social side of his nature, made possible by checking its selfish side. Requiring a person to obey strict rules of justice for the sake of others develops the feelings and capacities directed towards their good. But restraining him merely because they are displeased, in matters that do not affect their good, develops nothing valuable except whatever strength of character he may acquire in resisting the restraint. If he submits, it dulls and blunts his whole nature. To give each person's nature a fair chance, different people must be allowed to lead different lives. The extent to which an age has allowed this freedom has determined how noteworthy it has become to posterity. Even despotism does not produce its worst effects while Individuality survives beneath it. And whatever crushes individuality is despotism, whatever name it bears, and whether it claims to enforce God's will or human commands.

Having argued that Individuality is development itself, and that only the cultivation of individuality does or can produce fully developed human beings, I could end the argument here. What greater praise can any condition of human affairs receive than that it brings people closer to the best they can become? And what worse can be said of any obstacle to good than that it prevents this? Yet these considerations will surely fail to convince those most in need of conviction. We must therefore go further and show that developed human beings are useful to the undeveloped. Those who do not want liberty and would not use it must be shown some understandable benefit they themselves can gain from allowing others to exercise it without interference.

First, I would suggest that they might learn something from them. No one will deny that originality contributes something valuable to human affairs. We always need people to discover new truths and to show when things once true are no longer so. We also need people to begin new practices and demonstrate more enlightened conduct, better taste, and sounder sense in the conduct of life. Anyone who denies this must believe that the world's ways and practices have already reached perfection. Admittedly, not everyone can provide this benefit equally. Compared with humanity as a whole, few people conduct experiments that others could adopt with any prospect of improving on established practice. Yet these few are the salt of the earth; without them human life would stagnate like a pool. They not only introduce good things that did not exist before, but keep existing good things alive. If there were nothing new left to do, would human intelligence become unnecessary? Would that justify people in forgetting why the old things are done, and doing them like cattle instead of human beings? Even the best beliefs and practices are all too liable to become mechanical. Unless successive individuals brought fresh originality to prevent the grounds of those beliefs and practices from becoming mere tradition, this dead material could not withstand the slightest impact from anything truly alive. There would then be nothing to stop civilisation from dying out, as it did in the Byzantine Empire. People of genius are admittedly a small minority, and probably always will be. But if we are to have them, we must preserve the soil in which they grow. Genius can breathe freely only in an atmosphere of freedom. People of genius are, ex vi termini, more individual than anyone else. Consequently, they are less able to fit without damaging compression into the few moulds society supplies to spare its members the trouble of shaping their own characters. If timidity makes them accept being forced into one of these moulds, leaving undeveloped everything in themselves that cannot grow under the pressure, society will gain little from their genius. If their character is strong and they break their chains, the society that has failed to make them commonplace singles them out, with solemn warnings, as "wild," "erratic," and so forth. This is much like complaining that the Niagara river does not flow smoothly between its banks like a Dutch canal.

I stress so strongly both the importance of genius and its need for freedom to develop in thought and action because, although I know nobody will dispute this in theory, I also know that in practice almost everyone is entirely indifferent to it. People consider genius admirable when it allows someone to write an exciting poem or paint a picture. But genius in its true meaning--originality in thought and action--is something almost everyone secretly believes they can manage very well without, although no one openly denies that it deserves admiration. Unfortunately, this is too natural to be surprising. Originality is the one thing whose usefulness unoriginal minds cannot feel. They cannot see what it will do for them; how could they? If they could foresee what it would do, it would not be original. Its first service is to open their eyes. Once that has been fully accomplished, they would have a chance to become original themselves. Meanwhile, let them remember that nothing has ever been done without someone doing it first, and that every good thing in existence is a fruit of originality. Let them therefore have the modesty to believe that originality still has work to do, and recognise that the less aware they are of needing it, the greater their need.

The plain truth is that, whatever respect people profess or even show for real or supposed intellectual superiority, the general movement throughout the world is towards making mediocrity the dominant human power. In ancient history, in the middle ages, and to a diminishing extent during the long transition from feudal society to the present, an individual was a power in himself. If he possessed great talents or high social rank, that power was considerable. Today, individuals disappear into the crowd. In politics it is almost a commonplace to say that public opinion rules the world. The only power worthy of the name belongs to the masses, and to governments insofar as they become the instruments of the masses' tendencies and instincts. This holds as much for the moral and social relations of private life as for public affairs. The people whose opinions count as public opinion are not everywhere the same kind of public: in America they comprise the entire white population; in England they are chiefly the middle class. But they are always a mass--in other words, collective mediocrity. An even greater novelty is that the masses no longer receive their opinions from dignitaries of Church or State, from recognised leaders, or from books. People much like themselves do their thinking for them, addressing them or speaking in their name through newspapers, on the impulse of the moment. I am not complaining about all this. I do not claim that, given the present low state of the human mind, anything better is generally possible. But that does not make the rule of mediocrity anything other than mediocre government. No democracy or large aristocracy has ever risen, or could rise, above mediocrity in its political actions or in the opinions, qualities, and cast of mind it encourages, except insofar as the sovereign Many have accepted the guidance of the advice and influence of a more gifted and better educated One or Few. In their best periods they have always accepted such guidance. Every wise or noble undertaking begins, and must begin, with individuals, usually with one individual at first. The average person's honour and glory lies in his ability to follow that initiative: to respond inwardly to wise and noble things and be led towards them with his eyes open. I am not endorsing the kind of "hero-worship" that applauds a powerful man of genius for forcibly taking control of the world and compelling it to obey him against its will. He can claim only the freedom to point out the way. Power to force others along it is incompatible with their freedom and development, and also corrupts the powerful man himself. Yet when the opinions of masses of merely average people are everywhere becoming, or have already become, the dominant force, an increasingly pronounced individuality among those who reach the heights of thought would seem the necessary counterweight and correction. In these circumstances especially, exceptional people should be encouraged, rather than discouraged, to act differently from the mass. In other times, doing so was no benefit unless they acted better as well as differently. In our age, simply setting an example of nonconformity, simply refusing to bow to custom, performs a service. Precisely because opinion's tyranny makes eccentricity a reproach, people need to be eccentric to break that tyranny. Wherever and whenever strength of character has flourished, eccentricity has flourished too. A society's degree of eccentricity has generally matched its degree of genius, mental vigour, and moral courage. The chief danger of our time is revealed by how few people now dare to be eccentric.

I have argued that unfamiliar practices should be given the widest possible freedom, so that time may show which deserve to become customs. But independence in action and disregard for custom deserve encouragement for more than the chance they offer of discovering better ways to act and customs more worthy of general adoption. Nor is a just claim to live in one's own way confined to people of clearly superior intelligence. There is no reason why every human life should follow one pattern, or a small handful of patterns. Provided a person has a reasonable measure of common-sense and experience, his own way of arranging his life is best for him, not because it is best in itself, but because it is his own. Human beings are not sheep; and even sheep are not so alike that they cannot be distinguished. A man cannot find a coat or a pair of boots that fits unless it is made to measure or he has an entire warehouse to choose from. Is fitting him with a life easier than fitting him with a coat? Or are people more alike in their entire bodily and spiritual constitution than in the shape of their feet? Differences of taste alone would be sufficient reason not to try to shape everyone to a single model. But different people also need different conditions for their spiritual development. They can no more thrive in one moral atmosphere and climate than all varieties of plants can thrive in one physical atmosphere and climate. What helps one person cultivate his higher nature hinders another. A way of life that provides healthy stimulation for one, keeping all his capacities for action and enjoyment in excellent order, may burden and distract another, suspending or crushing his whole inner life. People differ so much in their sources of pleasure, their sensitivity to pain, and the effects that physical and moral influences have on them, that without a corresponding variety in their ways of life they cannot receive their fair share of happiness or reach the mental, moral, and aesthetic stature their nature permits. Why, then, should public feeling tolerate only those tastes and ways of life whose followers are numerous enough to force acceptance? Except in some monastic institutions, differences of taste are nowhere entirely denied. A person may like or dislike rowing, smoking, music, athletic exercises, chess, cards, or study without blame, because the people on either side are too numerous to suppress. Yet a man, and still more a woman, accused of doing "what nobody does," or not doing "what everybody does," attracts as much disparaging comment as though guilty of some grave moral offence. To enjoy even a little of the luxury of doing as they please without losing public esteem, people need a title or some other sign of rank, or of favour with people of rank. I repeat: even a little. Anyone who indulges much further risks worse than disparaging words--a commission de lunatico, and the transfer of their property to their relations.

One feature of public opinion's present direction makes it especially intolerant of any conspicuous display of individuality. People of the general average are moderate in their inclinations as well as in their intellect. They have no tastes or wishes strong enough to lead them to do anything unusual. They consequently fail to understand people who do, and class them with the wild and intemperate people they habitually despise. Add to this general fact a strong movement for moral improvement, and what we should expect becomes clear. Such a movement is now under way. It has already achieved much in making conduct more regular and discouraging excesses. A philanthropic spirit is also abroad, and no field invites its activity more readily than improving our fellow-creatures' morals and prudence. These tendencies make the public more willing than at most earlier periods to prescribe general rules of conduct and try to make everyone fit the approved standard. Whether stated or unspoken, that standard requires people to desire nothing strongly. Its ideal character has no distinctive character at all. It would compress and maim, like a Chinese lady's foot, every prominent part of human nature that might give a person a noticeably different outline from commonplace humanity.

As usually happens with ideals that exclude half of what is desirable, today's standard of approval produces only an inferior imitation of the remaining half. Instead of great energies directed by vigorous reason and strong feelings firmly governed by a conscientious will, it produces weak feelings and weak energies. These can be kept outwardly obedient to rules without strength of either will or reason. Already, energetic characters of any great scope are becoming little more than a memory handed down from the past. Business is now almost the only outlet for energy in this country. The energy devoted to it may still be called considerable. What little it leaves over goes into some hobby. The hobby may be useful, even philanthropic, but it is always a single pursuit, generally on a small scale. England's greatness is now entirely collective. Small as individuals, we seem capable of greatness only through our habit of combining, and our moral and religious philanthropists are perfectly satisfied with this. But it was people of a different kind who made England what it has been, and people of a different kind will be needed to keep it from declining.

Everywhere, the despotism of custom is the permanent obstacle to human advancement. It is constantly at war with the inclination to seek something better than the customary--an inclination called, according to circumstances, the spirit of liberty, progress, or improvement. The spirit of improvement does not always favour liberty: it may seek to force improvements on an unwilling people. And insofar as the spirit of liberty resists such efforts, it may temporarily and in particular places join forces with opponents of improvement. Yet liberty is the only unfailing, enduring source of improvement, because it makes every individual a possible independent centre of it. In either form, however--love of liberty or love of improvement--the progressive principle opposes the rule of Custom, since it requires at least release from that yoke. The struggle between them gives human history its chief interest. Strictly speaking, most of the world has no history, because Custom's despotism is complete. This is true throughout the East. There custom is the final authority in everything; justice and right mean conformity to it. No one thinks of resisting an appeal to custom, except perhaps a tyrant intoxicated with power. We can see the result. Those nations must once have possessed originality. They did not spring from the ground populous, literate, and skilled in many of life's arts. They made themselves so, and were then the world's greatest and most powerful nations. What are they today? Subjects or dependants of tribes whose ancestors wandered in forests when their own inhabited magnificent palaces and splendid temples--tribes among whom custom had to share its rule with liberty and progress. Apparently, a people can progress for a time and then stop. When does it stop? When it loses individuality. If Europe's nations undergo a similar change, it will not take exactly the same form. The despotism of custom threatening them does not precisely mean standing still. It forbids singularity but allows change, so long as everyone changes together. We have abandoned our ancestors' fixed costumes. Everyone must still dress like everyone else, but the fashion may change once or twice a year. In this way we ensure that change occurs for its own sake, rather than from any conception of beauty or convenience. The same conception of beauty or convenience would not occur to everyone at the same instant and then be discarded by everyone at another. Yet we are progressive as well as changeable. We constantly invent new mechanical devices and keep them until better ones replace them. We are eager to improve politics, education, and even morals, although in morals improvement mainly means persuading or forcing other people to be as good as ourselves. Progress is not what we object to: indeed, we flatter ourselves that no people has ever been so progressive. Our enemy is individuality. We would think we had achieved wonders if we made ourselves all alike. We forget that differences between people are generally what first draw either person's attention to the shortcomings of his own type, to another's superiority, or to the possibility of combining the strengths of both to create something better than either. China provides a warning example. It is a nation of considerable talent and, in some respects, even wisdom, thanks to the rare good fortune of receiving an unusually good set of customs early in its history. These were partly the work of men to whom even the most enlightened European must, with certain qualifications, grant the title of sages and philosophers. The Chinese are also remarkable for the excellence of their system for impressing their best wisdom, as far as possible, on every mind in the community, and ensuring that those who have absorbed most of it occupy positions of honour and power. Surely a people who achieved this must have discovered the secret of human progress and remained steadily at the forefront of the world's development. On the contrary, they have stood still for thousands of years; and if they are ever to improve further, it must be through foreigners. They have succeeded beyond all expectation in the very task to which English philanthropists apply themselves so diligently: making a whole people alike, all governing their thoughts and conduct by the same maxims and rules. These are the results. The modern rule of public opinion is the unorganised equivalent of China's organised educational and political systems. Unless individuality successfully resists this yoke, Europe, despite its noble past and its professed Christianity, will tend to become another China.

What has so far saved Europe from this fate? What has made the European family of nations a progressive rather than a stationary part of humanity? The answer is not any superior excellence they possess--where such excellence exists, it is an effect rather than a cause--but their remarkable variety of character and culture. Individuals, classes, and nations have differed enormously. They have pursued many different paths, each leading to something valuable. At every period, travellers on different paths have been intolerant of one another, and each would have welcomed the chance to force everyone else onto his own road. Yet their attempts to obstruct one another's development have seldom succeeded permanently, and each has eventually brought himself to accept the good the others offered. In my judgement, Europe owes its progressive, many-sided development entirely to this multiplicity of paths. But it is already enjoying considerably less of this benefit. It is clearly moving towards the Chinese ideal of making everyone alike. In his latest important work, M. de Tocqueville observes how much more alike today's Frenchmen are than those of even the previous generation. The observation would apply far more strongly to Englishmen. In the passage from Wilhelm von Humboldt quoted earlier, he identifies two necessary conditions of human development, necessary because they make people different from one another: freedom and variety of situations. In this country, the second condition is diminishing daily. The circumstances that surround different classes and individuals and shape their characters grow more alike every day. Once, different ranks, neighbourhoods, trades, and professions lived in what could be called different worlds; now, to a large extent, they inhabit the same one. Relatively speaking, they read, hear, and see the same things, visit the same places, direct their hopes and fears towards the same objects, and possess the same rights and liberties and the same means of asserting them. The differences of position that remain are great, but they are nothing beside those that have disappeared. And this levelling continues. Every political change of our age encourages it, since all tend to lift the low and lower the high. Every extension of education encourages it by subjecting people to shared influences and giving them access to the common stock of facts and sentiments. Better means of communication encourage it by bringing people from distant places into personal contact and sustaining a rapid movement of residents between places. Expanding commerce and manufactures encourage it by spreading the benefits of comfortable circumstances more widely and opening every object of ambition, even the highest, to general competition. The wish to rise thus becomes characteristic of every class, rather than of one. Still more powerful than all these forces in making people generally alike is the fully established supremacy of public opinion in the State, here and in other free countries. The social heights from which people could safely disregard the multitude's opinion are gradually being levelled. Practical politicians increasingly lose even the idea of resisting the public's will once it is definitely known to have one. As a result, nonconformity loses its social support: no substantial power remains within society that, being itself opposed to the supremacy of numbers, has an interest in protecting opinions and tendencies different from those of the public.

Together these causes produce such a weight of forces hostile to Individuality that it is hard to see how it can hold its ground. It will face increasing difficulty unless the intelligent part of the public can be brought to value it: to recognise that differences are good even when they are not improvements, and even when some appear to them to be changes for the worse. If the claims of Individuality are ever to be upheld, now is the time, while much remains to be done before enforced uniformity is complete. Resistance to this encroachment can succeed only in its earlier stages. The demand that everyone else resemble ourselves grows stronger as it is satisfied. If resistance waits until life has been reduced almost to a single pattern, every departure from that pattern will come to seem impious, immoral, even monstrous and unnatural. Once people have gone for some time without seeing diversity, they quickly lose the ability to imagine it.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Of the Limits to the Authority of Society Over the Individual
paragraphs: Where, then, should the individual's rightful sovereignty over himself end? At what point does society's authority begin? How much of a human life properly belongs to individuality, and how much properly belongs to society?

Each receives its rightful share when it is given what concerns it most directly. Individuality should govern the part of life in which the individual's interest predominates; society should govern the part in which society has the chief interest.

Society is not founded on a contract, and inventing one in order to derive social duties from it serves no useful purpose. Nevertheless, everyone protected by society owes something in return. Living in society makes it essential that each person be required to follow certain rules of conduct towards the others. First, people must not injure one another's interests--or, more precisely, those interests that should be recognised as rights, whether through an explicit legal provision or an unspoken understanding. Secondly, each must bear his share, determined by some fair principle, of the work and sacrifices needed to defend society or its members from injury and interference. Society is justified in enforcing these conditions, whatever the cost to those who try to evade them. Its authority does not end there. An individual's actions may harm others or show insufficient regard for their welfare without actually violating any of their established rights. In that case, public opinion may justly punish the offender, though the law may not. Once any part of someone's conduct adversely affects other people's interests, it comes within society's jurisdiction. We can then discuss whether intervention would promote the general welfare. But no such question arises where a person's conduct affects no one's interests but his own, or need affect others only if they choose--provided everyone concerned is of full age and has an ordinary level of understanding. In all these cases there should be complete freedom, both legal and social, to act and accept the consequences.

It would seriously misunderstand this doctrine to take it for selfish indifference: to suppose it says that people have no concern with one another's conduct, and should take no interest in one another's good behaviour or well-being unless their own interests are involved. We need far more unselfish effort to promote others' good, not less. But disinterested kindness can find ways to persuade people towards their own good other than whips and scourges, literal or metaphorical. I would be the last to undervalue the self-regarding virtues. They rank only second to the social virtues in importance, if indeed they rank second at all. Education should cultivate both equally. Even education, however, uses conviction and persuasion as well as compulsion; and once the period of education is over, only conviction and persuasion should be used to instil the self-regarding virtues. People owe one another help in distinguishing better from worse, and encouragement to choose the better and avoid the worse. They should continually encourage one another to exercise their higher faculties more fully, and to direct their feelings and aims towards objects and thoughts that are wise rather than foolish, elevating rather than degrading. Yet no person, and no number of people, is entitled to tell another mature human being that he may not use his life for his own benefit in the way he chooses. He has the greatest interest in his own well-being. Except where there is strong personal attachment, anyone else's interest in it is trifling beside his. Society's interest in him as an individual, apart from his conduct towards others, is small and wholly indirect. And even the most ordinary man or woman has means of knowing their own feelings and circumstances immeasurably better than anyone else can know them. When society overrides someone's judgement and purposes in matters concerning only himself, it must rely on general assumptions. These may be entirely wrong. Even when right, they are as likely as not to be wrongly applied to individual cases by people who know those circumstances only from the outside. This part of human affairs is therefore Individuality's proper field. In dealings between people, general rules must mostly be followed so that everyone can know what to expect. But in a person's own concerns, his individual spontaneity has a right to free exercise. Others may offer him considerations to assist his judgement and appeals to strengthen his will; they may even press these upon him. The final judgement, however, belongs to him. All the errors he is likely to make despite advice and warning are far outweighed by the harm of allowing others to force him towards what they consider his good.

I do not mean that a person's self-regarding merits or shortcomings should have no effect on how others feel about him. That is neither possible nor desirable. Someone outstanding in qualities that promote his own good deserves admiration to that extent: he comes that much closer to the ideal perfection of human nature. Someone gravely lacking in those qualities will evoke the opposite feeling. Certain degrees of folly, or of what might be called baseness or corruption of taste--though the phrase is open to objection--necessarily and properly make a person an object of distaste, or even, in extreme cases, contempt, without justifying any harm to him. Anyone possessing the opposite qualities in due strength could not help feeling this way. Without wronging anyone, a person may act so that we cannot help judging him, and feeling towards him, as a fool or a being of an inferior order. Since he would prefer to avoid that judgement and feeling, warning him in advance does him a service, just as warning him of any other unpleasant consequence he risks would do. Indeed, it would be better if we performed this service much more freely than present ideas of politeness allow: if we could honestly tell another person that we think him at fault without being thought rude or presumptuous. We are also entitled to act in various ways on an unfavourable opinion of someone, exercising our own individuality without oppressing his. We need not, for instance, seek his company. We may avoid it, though we should not make a display of doing so, because we have a right to choose the company we find most agreeable. We may warn others against him, and may even have a duty to do so, if we think his example or conversation likely to harm his companions.
