When offering optional kindnesses, we may prefer others to him, except in kindnesses directed towards his improvement. In these ways, someone can suffer severe penalties from others for faults that directly concern himself alone. But those penalties arise only as the natural, and as it were spontaneous, consequences of the faults; they are not deliberately inflicted as punishment. Someone who is rash, obstinate, or conceited; who cannot live within modest means or restrain harmful indulgences; who pursues animal pleasures at the expense of pleasures of feeling and intellect--such a person must expect others to think less of him and feel less favourably towards him. He has no right to complain, unless exceptional merit in his relations with others has earned their favour and established a claim to their kindness that his faults towards himself do not diminish.

My contention is that, for the part of someone's conduct and character that concerns his own good without affecting others' interests in their relations with him, he should suffer only those disadvantages strictly inseparable from their unfavourable judgement. Actions that injure others call for wholly different treatment. Violating their rights; inflicting loss or damage not justified by one's own rights; lying or dealing deceitfully with them; exploiting advantages over them unfairly or ungenerously; even selfishly refusing to defend them against injury--all these properly invite moral condemnation and, in serious cases, moral retribution and punishment. The dispositions that lead to such acts, as well as the acts themselves, are truly immoral and deserve disapproval that may reach abhorrence. A cruel disposition; malice and ill-nature; envy, that most anti-social and hateful of passions; concealment and insincerity; anger without sufficient cause, and resentment beyond the provocation; a love of dominating others; the wish to seize more than one's share of advantages, the Greeks' [Greek: pleonexia]; pride that takes pleasure in others' humiliation; egotism that rates oneself and one's concerns above everything else and settles every doubtful question in one's own favour--these are moral vices, making up a bad and hateful moral character. They differ from the self-regarding faults mentioned earlier, which are not properly immoral and do not become wickedness however far they go. Such faults may reveal any degree of folly, or lack of personal dignity and self-respect. But they deserve moral condemnation only when they entail a failure of duty towards others for whose sake the individual is obliged to care for himself. What we call duties to ourselves are not obligations enforceable by society unless circumstances make them duties to others as well. When the expression duty to oneself means more than prudence, it means self-respect or self-development. None of these makes a person answerable to his fellow-creatures, because holding him answerable to them for any of them does not benefit humanity.

The distinction between the esteem a person may rightly lose through lack of prudence or personal dignity and the condemnation he deserves for violating others' rights is more than a distinction in name. Whether he displeases us in matters where we believe we may control him, or in matters where we know we may not, makes an enormous difference to both our feelings and our behaviour towards him. If he displeases us, we may show our distaste and keep away from him, just as we may avoid an unpleasant thing. But this does not call on us to make his life uncomfortable. We should remember that he already bears, or will bear, the full penalty of his mistake. If he ruins his life by managing it badly, that is no reason for us to want to ruin it further. Instead of wanting to punish him, we should try to lessen his punishment by showing him how to prevent or remedy the troubles his conduct is likely to cause. We may pity him, perhaps dislike him, but we should not feel anger or resentment. We should not treat him as society's enemy. The worst we should consider ourselves entitled to do is leave him alone, if we do not helpfully intervene by showing interest or concern. The situation is entirely different if he has broken rules necessary to protect his fellow-creatures, individually or collectively. Then the harmful consequences of his actions fall on others, not on himself. Society, as protector of all its members, must respond against him; it must inflict suffering expressly as punishment, and ensure that the punishment is severe enough. In this case he is an offender before our court, and we are called upon both to judge him and, in one form or another, to carry out our sentence. In the other case, we have no business inflicting suffering on him, except what may incidentally result from exercising the same freedom in our own affairs that we allow him in his.

Many people will reject the distinction I have drawn between the part of a life that concerns only the person living it and the part that concerns others. How, they may ask, can any conduct by a member of society be of no concern to the rest? Nobody exists in complete isolation. A person cannot seriously or permanently harm himself without the harm reaching at least those close to him, and often much further. If he damages his property, he harms those directly or indirectly supported by it, and usually reduces the community's total resources to some extent. If he impairs his bodily or mental faculties, he harms everyone who depends on him for any part of their happiness. He also makes himself unable to perform the services he owes his fellow-creatures generally, and may become a burden on their affection or kindness. If such conduct became very common, scarcely any offence would subtract more from the total good. Finally, it may be argued, even if someone's vices or follies do others no direct harm, his example is nevertheless harmful. He should therefore be forced to restrain himself for the sake of those who might be corrupted or misled by seeing or learning of his conduct.

The objection will go further: even if the consequences of misconduct could be confined to the vicious or thoughtless individual, should society leave people to guide themselves when they are plainly unfit to do so? We admit that children and those under age should be protected from themselves; is society not equally obliged to protect adults just as incapable of governing themselves? If gambling, drunkenness, incontinence, idleness, or uncleanliness damage happiness and obstruct improvement as much as many or most acts forbidden by law, why should the law not try to suppress them too, as far as practicality and social convenience allow? And to supplement the law's unavoidable shortcomings, should not opinion at least organise a powerful police against these vices and impose strict social penalties on those known to practise them? This, it may be said, has nothing to do with restricting individuality or preventing new and original experiments in living. The only things to be prevented are those tried and condemned from the world's beginning to the present, things experience has shown to be neither useful nor suitable for anyone's individuality. Surely there is some length of time and quantity of experience after which a moral or prudential truth can be considered established. The aim is simply to keep generation after generation from falling over the same precipice that destroyed their predecessors.

I fully accept that the harm a person does himself may seriously affect those close to him, both in their feelings and in their interests, and affect society at large to a lesser degree. If such conduct leads him to break a definite, identifiable obligation to another person or persons, the case ceases to be merely self-regarding and properly becomes subject to moral disapproval. Suppose a man becomes unable to pay his debts through intemperance or extravagance; or, having accepted moral responsibility for a family, becomes unable for the same reason to support or educate them. He deserves condemnation and may justly be punished, but for failing in his duty to his family or creditors, not for being extravagant. His moral guilt would be the same had he diverted the resources due to them into the most prudent investment. George Barnwell murdered his uncle to obtain money for his mistress; he would equally have been hanged had he done it to establish himself in business. Again, a man who, as often happens, grieves his family through addiction to bad habits deserves reproach for unkindness or ingratitude. But he may deserve the same reproach for cultivating habits that are not themselves vicious, if they distress those with whom he lives or those whose personal ties make them dependent on him for comfort. Anyone who fails to show the consideration generally owed to others' interests and feelings deserves moral disapproval for that failure, unless a more pressing duty compels him or a permissible preference for himself justifies him. But the disapproval is for the failure, not its cause, nor for purely personal errors that may have led to it indirectly. Similarly, someone who through purely self-regarding conduct makes himself unable to perform a definite duty to the public commits a social offence. Nobody should be punished simply for being drunk, but a soldier or policeman should be punished for being drunk on duty. In short, whenever an individual or the public suffers definite damage, or a definite risk of damage, the case passes from the domain of liberty into that of morality or law.

But consider the merely possible, or what might be called constructive, injury a person does society through conduct that breaks no specific duty to the public and causes no identifiable person except himself any perceptible harm. Society can afford this disadvantage for the greater good of human freedom. If adults are to be punished for failing to care properly for themselves, I would rather it be done for their own sake than under the pretence of preserving their ability to give society benefits that society does not claim a right to demand. Nor can I agree to discuss the question as though society had no way of bringing its weaker members up to its ordinary standard of rational conduct except waiting for them to act irrationally and then punishing them legally or morally. Society has held absolute power over the whole early part of their lives. It has had their entire childhood and minority in which to try to prepare them to conduct their lives rationally. The present generation controls both the training and the entire circumstances of the next. It cannot make them perfectly wise and good, for it is itself so sadly deficient in wisdom and goodness; nor are its best efforts always the most successful in individual cases. But it can certainly make the rising generation as a whole as good as itself, and a little better. If society allows any large number of its members to grow up mere children, unable to respond to rational consideration of distant consequences, it has itself to blame for what follows. Society possesses not only all the powers of education, but the influence that an accepted opinion always exerts over minds least able to judge for themselves. It also has the help of the natural penalties that inevitably fall on those who earn the distaste or contempt of their acquaintances. Armed with all this, society should not pretend that it also needs the power to command and enforce obedience in personal concerns, where every principle of justice and practical policy gives the decision to those who must bear the consequences. Nothing, moreover, does more to discredit and defeat the better ways of influencing conduct than resorting to worse ones. If those whom society tries to force into prudence or temperance have any of the material of vigorous, independent character in them, they will certainly rebel against the yoke. No such person will ever feel that others have the same right to control his own concerns as they have to keep him from injuring theirs. Defying this usurped authority, and ostentatiously doing the exact opposite of what it commands, can readily become a sign of spirit and courage. So it was with the fashion for grossness under Charles II. that followed the Puritans' fanatical moral intolerance. As for the alleged need to protect society against the bad examples of vicious or self-indulgent people, a bad example can indeed be harmful, especially the example of wronging others without punishment. But the conduct we are discussing wrongs no one else and is supposed to inflict great harm on the person himself. I cannot see how anyone who believes that can avoid concluding that the example must, on balance, be more beneficial than harmful. For alongside the misconduct it displays the painful or degrading consequences which, if the conduct deserves censure, must be assumed to accompany it in all or most cases.

The strongest argument against public interference with purely personal conduct is that, when the public interferes, it will probably do so wrongly and in the wrong matters. On questions of social morality and duties to others, public opinion--that is, the opinion of a dominant majority--may often be wrong, but is likely to be right still more often. On these questions people need only judge their own interests: how allowing a particular kind of conduct would affect them. But when a similar majority imposes its opinion as law on a minority in matters of self-regarding conduct, that opinion is as likely to be wrong as right. At best it represents some people's judgement of what benefits or harms other people. Often it does not even represent that. The public simply disregards, with complete indifference, the pleasure or convenience of those it censures, and considers its own preferences alone. Many people treat any conduct they dislike as an injury to themselves, resenting it as an outrage against their feelings. A religious bigot accused of disregarding others' religious feelings has been known to answer that they disregard his by persisting in their abominable worship or creed. But a person's feeling for his own opinion and another person's offence at his holding it are not equal claims, any more than a thief's wish to take a purse equals its rightful owner's wish to keep it. A person's taste is as much his own concern as his opinion or his purse. Anyone can imagine an ideal public that leaves individual freedom and choice untouched in uncertain matters, and requires abstention only from conduct condemned by universal experience. But where has any public ever limited its censorship in this way? When does it trouble to consult universal experience? In interfering with personal conduct, it seldom thinks of anything except the enormity of acting or feeling differently from itself. Nine-tenths of moralists and speculative writers present this barely disguised standard of judgement to humanity as the command of religion and philosophy. They teach that things are right because they are right--because we feel them to be so. They tell us to look into our own minds and hearts for laws of conduct binding on ourselves and everyone else. What can the poor public do but follow these instructions, and impose its personal feelings about good and evil on the whole world whenever it is reasonably united in them?

The evil I have described is not merely theoretical. I may therefore be expected to identify cases in which the public of our own time and country wrongly turns its preferences into moral laws. I am not writing an essay on the errors of current moral feeling; that subject is too serious to treat in passing as an illustration. Yet examples are needed to show that the principle I defend has real practical importance, and that I am not building a barrier against imaginary evils. It is easy to supply abundant instances showing that one of the most widespread human tendencies is to extend what we may call moral policing until it trespasses on the individual's most unquestionably rightful liberty.

Consider first the hostilities people feel for no better reason than that those of another religion do not observe their religious practices, especially their abstinences. To take a rather trivial example, nothing in Christian belief or practice does more to embitter Mahomedans' hatred than Christians' eating pork. Christians and Europeans regard few acts with greater unfeigned disgust than Mussulmans feel for this way of satisfying hunger. It offends against their religion, certainly, but this does not explain either the intensity or the particular nature of their revulsion. Their religion also forbids wine, and all Mussulmans consider drinking it wrong, but not disgusting. Their aversion to the flesh of the "unclean beast," by contrast, has the special quality of an instinctive antipathy. Once the idea of uncleanness has sunk deeply into the feelings, it seems always to produce this kind of aversion, even in people whose personal habits are far from scrupulously clean. The feeling of religious impurity, so intense among the Hindoos, is a striking example. Now suppose that a country's majority were Mussulmans and insisted that nobody within its borders be allowed to eat pork. This would be nothing new in Mahomedan countries. Would it be a legitimate exercise of public opinion's moral authority? If not, why not? That public truly finds the practice revolting, and sincerely believes the Deity forbids and abhors it. Nor could the ban be condemned as religious persecution. Its origin might be religious, but it would not persecute anyone for religion, since no one's religion imposes a duty to eat pork. The only sustainable ground for condemning it would be that the public has no business interfering with individuals' personal tastes and self-regarding concerns.

To turn a little nearer home, most Spaniards consider worship in any form other than the Roman Catholic a grave impiety, supremely offensive to the Supreme Being; and no other public worship is legal on Spanish soil. Throughout Southern Europe, people regard married clergy as not merely irreligious but unchaste, indecent, gross, and disgusting. What do Protestants think of these entirely sincere feelings and the effort to enforce them on non-Catholics? Yet if people may justifiably interfere with one another's liberty in matters that do not affect others' interests, what principle can consistently exclude these cases? Who can blame people for wanting to suppress what they see as scandalous before God and man? To those who consider these practices impious, the case for suppressing them is as strong as any case against supposed personal immorality can be. Unless we are prepared to adopt the persecutor's reasoning--that we may persecute others because we are right, but they may not persecute us because they are wrong--we must take care not to accept a principle whose application to ourselves we would resent as a gross injustice.

Someone may object, though unreasonably, that the preceding examples involve circumstances impossible here. Opinion in this country is unlikely to enforce abstinence from particular meats, or to interfere with people for worshipping, marrying, or remaining unmarried according to their beliefs or inclinations. My next example, however, concerns an interference with liberty whose danger we have certainly not escaped. Wherever the Puritans have gained sufficient power--as in New England and in Great Britain under the Commonwealth--they have tried, with considerable success, to suppress all public and almost all private amusements. They especially targeted music, dancing, public games and other gatherings for entertainment, and the theatre. Large groups in this country still condemn these recreations on moral and religious grounds. They belong chiefly to the middle class, the dominant power under the kingdom's present social and political conditions, so it is entirely possible that people holding such views may one day command a parliamentary majority. How would the rest of the community enjoy having its permitted amusements determined by the religious and moral feelings of strict Calvinists and Methodists? Would it not insist, rather firmly, that these intrusively pious people mind their own business? That is exactly what should be said to any government or public claiming that nobody may enjoy a pleasure it considers wrong. But once the principle behind that claim is accepted, no one can reasonably object to its being applied according to the views of the majority or whatever other power predominates in the country. Everyone must then be prepared to live under the early New England settlers' conception of a Christian commonwealth, if a religious profession like theirs ever regains its lost ground--as religions thought to be declining have so often done.

Consider another possibility, perhaps more likely than the last. There is admittedly a strong tendency in the modern world towards a democratic organisation of society, whether or not popular political institutions accompany it. In the United States, where this tendency has gone furthest and both society and government are most democratic, it is said that the majority's feelings operate like a fairly effective sumptuary law. They dislike any display of a costlier or more splendid way of life than they can hope to rival. In many parts of the Union, it is said, someone with a very large income struggles to find any way of spending it that does not provoke popular disapproval. Such reports undoubtedly exaggerate present conditions considerably. Yet what they describe is not only conceivable and possible but a probable result of combining democratic feeling with the belief that the public may veto how individuals spend their incomes. Add a widespread acceptance of Socialist opinions, and the majority may come to regard owning more than a very small amount of property, or receiving any income not earned by manual labour, as disgraceful. Opinions based on similar principles already prevail widely among artisans, bearing oppressively on those chiefly answerable to that class's opinion--its own members. It is known that the bad workmen who constitute the majority of workers in many industries firmly believe that bad workmen should receive the same wages as good ones. They believe no one should be allowed, through piecework or otherwise, to earn by greater skill or diligence more than others can earn without it. They enforce this belief through moral policing, occasionally becoming physical, to deter skilled workers from accepting, and employers from paying, higher wages for more useful service. If the public has any authority over private concerns, I cannot see how these people are at fault. Nor can I see how the particular public surrounding an individual can be blamed for claiming the same authority over his conduct that the general public claims over people at large.

But we need not dwell on hypothetical cases. In our own time, gross invasions of private liberty actually occur, and still greater ones are threatened with some prospect of success. Views are being advanced that give the public an unlimited right to prohibit by law whatever it considers wrong--and, to reach what it considers wrong, to prohibit any number of things it admits are innocent.

In the name of preventing intemperance, the people of one English colony and nearly half the United States have been legally forbidden any use of fermented drinks except for medical purposes. For banning their sale is in practice, and by intention, banning their use. The difficulty of enforcing the law has led several States that adopted it to repeal it, including the State that gave it its name. Nevertheless, many professed philanthropists have begun an energetic campaign for a similar law here. The association formed for this purpose, which calls itself an "Alliance", has attracted some attention through published correspondence between its Secretary and one of the very few English public men who believe a politician's opinions should rest on principles. Lord Stanley's contribution to that exchange should strengthen the hopes already placed in him by those who know how regrettably rare the qualities displayed in some of his public appearances are among people in political life. The Alliance's spokesman, who would "deeply deplore the recognition of any principle which could be wrested to justify bigotry and persecution," sets out to identify the "broad and impassable barrier" separating such principles from the association's own. "All matters relating to thought, opinion, conscience, appear to me," he says, "to be without the sphere of legislation; all pertaining to social act, habit, relation, subject only to a discretionary power vested in the State itself, and not in the individual, to be within it." He says nothing of a third category distinct from both: acts and habits that are individual rather than social. Surely drinking fermented liquors belongs in this category. Selling them, however, is trade, and trade is a social act. But the liberty at issue is the buyer's and consumer's, not the seller's. The State might as well forbid a person to drink wine as deliberately make it impossible for him to obtain any. The Secretary nevertheless says, "I claim, as a citizen, a right to legislate whenever my social rights are invaded by the social act of another." Now comes the definition of these "social rights." "If anything invades my social rights, certainly the traffic in strong drink does. It destroys my primary right of security, by constantly creating and stimulating social disorder. It invades my right of equality, by deriving a profit from the creation of a misery, I am taxed to support. It impedes my right to free moral and intellectual development, by surrounding my path with dangers, and by weakening and demoralising society, from which I have a right to claim mutual aid and intercourse." Here is a theory of "social rights," probably unlike anything ever before stated explicitly. It amounts to an absolute social right for every individual to have every other individual behave exactly as he ought in every respect. Anyone who fails in the smallest detail violates my social right and entitles me to demand a legislative remedy. Such a monstrous principle is far more dangerous than any single interference with liberty. It could justify every conceivable violation. It recognises no right to freedom at all, except perhaps to hold opinions secretly and never disclose them. The instant anyone voices an opinion I consider harmful, it violates all the "social rights" the Alliance assigns to me. This doctrine gives everyone a vested interest in everyone else's moral, intellectual, and even physical perfection, with each claimant defining perfection by his own standard.

Another important example of unjustified interference with the individual's rightful liberty, long since successfully imposed rather than merely threatened, is Sabbatarian legislation. Resting from one's usual daily occupation one day a week, as far as life's necessities permit, is undoubtedly a very beneficial custom, though it is a religious obligation only for Jews. The custom requires general agreement among the working classes. Where some people's working would oblige others to work too, it may therefore be permissible and right for the law to suspend the principal industrial activities on a particular day, guaranteeing each person that others will observe the custom. But this justification rests on the direct interest people have in one another's observance. It does not apply to activities someone freely chooses for his leisure, and cannot justify legal restrictions on amusements at all. Admittedly, one person's amusement is another's day's work. But the pleasure of many--to say nothing of beneficial recreation--is worth the labour of a few, provided that work is freely chosen and can freely be given up. Workers are entirely right to think that if everyone worked on Sunday, seven days' work would have to be done for six days' wages. But while most work is suspended, the few who must work for others' enjoyment receive a proportionate increase in earnings. They need not remain in those occupations if they prefer leisure to pay. A further remedy, if wanted, could be a customary holiday on another weekday for these particular groups. Restrictions on Sunday amusements can therefore be defended only on the ground that such amusements are religiously wrong. We cannot protest too strongly against using this as a basis for legislation. "Deorum injuriae Diis curae." It has yet to be shown that society or its officials have a commission from heaven to avenge a supposed offence against Omnipotence that does not also wrong our fellow-creatures. The idea that one person has a duty to make another religious underlay every religious persecution ever committed, and accepting it would fully justify them all. The feeling behind repeated efforts to stop Sunday railway travel, resist the opening of Museums, and so forth lacks the old persecutors' cruelty, but reveals fundamentally the same state of mind. It refuses to tolerate others doing what their own religion permits because the persecutor's religion forbids it. It assumes that God not only abhors the misbeliever's act, but will hold us guilty if we leave him undisturbed.

To these examples of the scant regard commonly paid to human liberty, I must add the language of outright persecution that erupts in this country's press whenever it feels obliged to discuss the remarkable phenomenon of Mormonism. Much could be said about the unexpected and instructive fact that, in the age of newspapers, railways, and the electric telegraph, hundreds of thousands believe an alleged new revelation and the religion founded on it, and have made it the basis of a society. The religion is the product of obvious imposture, unsupported even by the prestige of exceptional qualities in its founder. What concerns us here is that this religion, like other and better religions, has its martyrs. A mob killed its prophet and founder for his teaching; other believers died through the same lawless violence; and the believers were forcibly expelled as a body from the country where they first arose. Now that they have been driven into an isolated retreat in a desert, many people here openly declare that sending an expedition to force them to conform to others' opinions would be right, though inconvenient. The Mormonite doctrine chiefly responsible for the hostility that overrides ordinary religious tolerance is its approval of polygamy. Though allowed to Mahomedans, Hindoos, and Chinese, polygamy seems to arouse inexhaustible hatred when practised by English speakers who profess a kind of Christianity. No one disapproves more deeply than I do of this Mormon institution. Among other objections, it directly violates the principle of liberty, rather than receiving any support from it: it simply fastens the chains of half the community more securely while releasing the other half from reciprocal obligations towards them. Still, we must remember that the women involved, whom we may regard as its sufferers, enter this relationship as voluntarily as women enter any other form of marriage. Surprising as this may seem, ordinary ideas and customs explain it. By teaching women that marriage is the one essential thing, they make it understandable that many women would prefer being one of several wives to being no one's wife. Other countries are not asked to recognise these unions or exempt any inhabitants from their own laws because of Mormonite beliefs. But these dissenters have conceded far more to others' hostility than could justly be demanded. They have left the countries where their doctrines were unwelcome and settled in a remote corner of the earth that they were the first to make habitable. On what grounds other than tyranny could they be prevented from living there under laws of their choice, provided they attack no other nation and give anyone dissatisfied with their ways complete freedom to leave? A recent writer of considerable merit in some respects proposes, in his own words, not a crusade but a civilizade against this polygamous community, to end what he regards as a backward step in civilisation. I also regard it as such, but I know of no right by which one community may force another to be civilised. Unless those suffering under the bad law ask other communities for help, I cannot accept that people entirely unconnected with them should intervene. They should not demand an end to conditions apparently satisfying everyone directly concerned merely because those conditions scandalise people thousands of miles away who have no part or concern in them. Let them send missionaries to preach against it if they wish. Let them also use any fair means--silencing its teachers is not one--to resist similar doctrines spreading among their own people. If civilisation defeated barbarism when barbarism had the world to itself, it is too much to profess fear that defeated barbarism will rise again and conquer civilisation. A civilisation capable of succumbing to its vanquished enemy must first have become so degenerate that neither its appointed priests and teachers nor anyone else can defend it or will take the trouble to do so. If that is the case, the sooner such a civilisation is given notice to quit, the better. It can only deteriorate until energetic barbarians destroy and regenerate it, as they did the Western Empire.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Applications
paragraphs: Before we can usefully attempt to apply these principles consistently across every area of government and morality, they must be more widely accepted as the basis for discussing particular questions. The few observations on details that I propose here are intended to illustrate the principles, rather than trace all their consequences. I offer examples of application rather than a complete set of applications. They may help clarify the meaning and limits of the two maxims that together make up this Essay's entire doctrine, and help us balance them in cases where it is uncertain which should apply.

The first maxim is that individuals are not answerable to society for actions that concern nobody's interests but their own. Society can justifiably express disapproval or dislike of such conduct only through advice, instruction, persuasion, or avoidance by people who consider avoidance necessary for their own good. The second maxim is that individuals are answerable for actions harmful to others' interests. They may be subjected to social or legal penalties if society believes either kind of punishment is necessary to protect itself.

First, we must not suppose that because harm, or the likelihood of harm, to others' interests is the only possible justification for society's intervention, it always justifies intervention. Pursuing a legitimate aim often necessarily, and therefore legitimately, causes others pain or loss, or deprives them of a benefit they reasonably hoped to obtain. These conflicts of interest often arise from bad social institutions, but remain unavoidable while those institutions last; some would be unavoidable under any institutions. Anyone succeeding in an overcrowded profession or a competitive examination, or chosen over another person for something both want, benefits from others' loss, wasted effort, and disappointment. Yet everyone generally accepts that humanity's common interest is better served when people pursue their aims undeterred by such consequences. In other words, society recognises no legal or moral right of disappointed competitors to escape this kind of suffering. It intervenes only when success is pursued by means that the general interest cannot permit: fraud or treachery, and force.

Trade, again, is a social act. Anyone selling goods of any kind to the public affects other people's interests and those of society generally. His conduct therefore falls in principle within society's jurisdiction. Governments were accordingly once thought responsible for fixing prices and regulating manufacturing methods in every case considered important. After a long struggle, however, it is now recognised that low prices and good quality are best secured by leaving producers and sellers completely free, checked only by buyers' equal freedom to buy elsewhere. This is the so-called doctrine of Free Trade. The grounds on which this doctrine rests are different from the grounds of the principle of individual liberty I have defended in this Essay, although they are equally solid. Restrictions on trade, or on production for trade, are certainly restraints, and restraint qua restraint is an evil. But these restrictions concern only conduct that society is entitled to restrain. They are wrong solely because they do not actually achieve their intended results. Just as Free Trade itself does not rest on individual liberty, most questions about its limits do not involve that principle either. Examples include how much public control is permissible to prevent fraudulent adulteration, or how far employers should be compelled to take sanitary precautions or protect workers in dangerous occupations. Liberty enters these questions only insofar as leaving people alone is always better, caeteris paribus, than controlling them. In principle, their legitimate subjection to control for these purposes is undeniable. Other interventions in trade, however, are fundamentally questions of liberty: the Maine Law already discussed, the ban on importing opium into China, restrictions on selling poisons--in short, every intervention intended to make a particular commodity impossible or difficult to obtain. Such measures are objectionable because they infringe the buyer's liberty, rather than the producer's or seller's.

One example, the sale of poisons, raises a new question: the proper limits of what we may call police functions, and how far liberty may legitimately be restricted to prevent crime or accidents. Government unquestionably has a duty to take precautions against crime before it occurs, as well as to detect and punish it afterwards. But its preventive function is far more open to abuse at liberty's expense than its punitive function. Scarcely any legitimate human freedom of action cannot be represented, with some justice, as making some kind of wrongdoing easier. Nevertheless, if a public authority or even a private person sees someone plainly preparing a crime, they need not stand inactive until it occurs: they may intervene to prevent it. If poisons were bought and used only for murder, banning their manufacture and sale would be right. But they can serve useful as well as innocent purposes, and restrictions on one use necessarily affect the other. Preventing accidents is also a proper task of public authority. If an official or anyone else saw someone about to cross a bridge known to be unsafe, with no time to warn him, they could seize him and turn him back without truly infringing his liberty. Liberty means doing what one wants, and he does not want to fall into the river. Where harm is only a risk rather than a certainty, however, only the person concerned can judge whether his reason for taking the risk is sufficient. I therefore think he should merely be warned, not forcibly prevented from exposing himself to danger, unless he is a child, delirious, or so excited or absorbed that he cannot fully exercise reflection. Applied to the sale of poisons, similar considerations help distinguish regulations that respect the principle from those that violate it. Requiring a drug to carry a label indicating its dangerous nature, for example, need not violate liberty: the buyer cannot wish to remain ignorant of its poisonous qualities. But demanding a medical practitioner's certificate in every case would always make legitimate access expensive and sometimes make it impossible. I see only one way to obstruct crime committed by this means without any significant infringement of the freedom of people wanting the substance for other purposes: provide what Bentham aptly calls "preappointed evidence." Everyone is familiar with provision of this sort in the case of contracts. When two parties enter a contract, it is both usual and right for the law to require them to observe certain formalities before it will enforce their promised performance. These may include their signatures, the attestation of witnesses, and other formalities of the same kind. If a dispute later arises, evidence will establish that the contract was genuinely made and that no circumstances rendered it legally invalid. This creates substantial obstacles to fictitious contracts and to contracts made under circumstances that, if known, would invalidate them. Similar precautions could govern sales of articles usable as instruments of crime. Sellers might have to register the transaction's exact time, the buyer's name and address, and the precise quality and quantity sold. They might have to ask the intended purpose and record the answer. If the buyer has no medical prescription, the presence of a third person could also be made a requirement of the sale. This would enable the fact of the purchase to be established against the purchaser if there were later grounds for believing that the article had been put to a criminal use. Such rules would generally pose no substantial obstacle to obtaining the article, but a considerable obstacle to misusing it without discovery.

Society's inherent right to protect itself against crime through advance precautions suggests obvious limits to the rule against preventing or punishing purely self-regarding misconduct. Drunkenness, for example, ordinarily gives legislation no proper occasion to intervene. But if someone has once been convicted of violence against others while drunk, I would consider a special legal restriction applying to that individual entirely legitimate. If he were subsequently found drunk, the law could make him liable to a penalty for being in that condition. If, while in that condition, he committed a further offence, the punishment to which that further offence exposed him could be increased in severity. For someone whose drunkenness provokes harm to others, becoming drunk is itself a crime against them. Likewise, idleness cannot be legally punished without tyranny, except where the person receives public support or where the idleness breaches a contract. But if idleness or any other avoidable cause makes a man neglect legal duties to others, such as supporting his children, forcing him to fulfil the obligation is not tyranny. If no other means exist, compulsory labour may be used to secure its fulfilment.

Many actions directly harm only the people performing them and therefore should not be legally forbidden. Done publicly, however, they may violate good manners and so become offences against others, which can rightfully be prohibited. Offences against decency belong here. We need not dwell on them, especially since their connection with our subject is only indirect: the objection to public performance applies equally strongly to many actions that are neither blameworthy in themselves nor considered so.

Another question requires an answer consistent with our principles. Suppose personal conduct is considered blameworthy, yet respect for liberty prevents society from stopping or punishing it because its direct harm falls entirely on the person acting. Should others be equally free to advise or encourage him to do what he is free to do? The answer presents difficulties. Urging someone else to act is not strictly self-regarding conduct. Advice and inducements are social acts and might therefore seem subject to social control, like other actions affecting people. A little reflection corrects that initial impression. Even if the case falls outside the strict definition of individual liberty, the reasons supporting that principle still apply. If people must be allowed to act as they think best in their own concerns, at their own risk, they must also be free to consult one another about what to do, exchange opinions, and give and receive suggestions. Whatever may be done may also be recommended. Doubt arises only when the person encouraging it benefits personally from his advice, making a livelihood or profit from promoting what society and the State consider an evil. At this point a genuinely new element complicates the question. There now exist whole classes of people with an interest opposed to what society regards as its common welfare, and their manner of earning a living depends on counteracting that welfare. Should society intervene? Fornication and gambling, for instance, must be tolerated; but should someone be free to act as a pimp or run a gambling-house? Such cases lie precisely on the boundary between two principles, and their proper place is not immediately clear. Both sides have arguments. For tolerance, one may say that making an occupation or livelihood of something cannot turn an otherwise permissible act into a crime. It should consistently be allowed or consistently prohibited. If the principles defended here are sound, society as a collective body has no business declaring wrong an act that concerns only the individual. It may dissuade but go no further, and one person should be as free to persuade as another to dissuade. Against this, one may argue that although neither the public nor the State may authoritatively pronounce purely individual conduct good or bad for purposes of suppression or punishment, they may regard its goodness or badness as at least debatable if they consider it bad. On that assumption, they cannot be wrong to exclude interested solicitations from people incapable of impartiality--people with a direct personal stake on the side the State considers wrong, who admittedly promote it solely for their own purposes. Surely nothing good is sacrificed by arranging that people choose, wisely or foolishly, on their own initiative, as free as possible from people skilfully stimulating their inclinations for private gain. Thus, it may be argued, laws against unlawful games are indefensible, and everyone should be free to gamble in their own or one another's homes, or at meeting places supported by their own subscriptions and open only to members and guests. Yet public gambling-houses should not be allowed. Admittedly, prohibition never works completely. Whatever tyrannical powers police receive, gambling-houses can always operate under some pretext. But they can be forced into enough secrecy that only those seeking them know of them, and society should aim at nothing more. There is considerable force in the arguments on this side, and I do not venture to decide whether their force is sufficient to justify the moral anomaly involved. The accessory would be punished while the principal actor is, and under our principles must be, allowed to go free. A procurer could be fined or imprisoned while the fornicator is not; the keeper of a gambling-house could be fined or imprisoned while the gambler is not. Still less should ordinary buying and selling be restricted on similar grounds. Almost everything sold can be used excessively, and sellers profit from encouraging excess. But that supplies no argument for the Maine Law, for example, because sellers of strong drink, though interested in its abuse, are indispensable to its legitimate use. Their interest in encouraging intemperance is nevertheless a real evil. That interest justifies the State in imposing restrictions and requiring guarantees from these dealers which, in the absence of this particular justification, would be infringements of their legitimate liberty.

A further question is whether the State, while permitting conduct it considers contrary to a person's best interests, should nevertheless discourage it indirectly. Should it, for example, make the means of drunkenness more expensive, or harder to obtain by limiting the number of outlets? As with most practical questions, several distinctions are necessary. Taxing stimulants solely to make them harder to obtain differs from complete prohibition only in degree, and is justified only if prohibition itself is justified. Every price increase prohibits purchase for those unable to afford the higher price. For those who can afford it, the increase is a penalty for satisfying a particular taste. Once people have met their legal and moral obligations to the State and to individuals, their choice of pleasures and manner of spending their income belong to them and must be left to their judgement. At first this may seem to rule out selecting stimulants for special taxation to raise revenue. But taxation for revenue is unavoidable. In most countries a considerable part must be indirect, so the State cannot avoid imposing penalties on the consumption of some goods, penalties that may prevent some people from buying them. When choosing taxes, the State must therefore consider which commodities consumers can most easily forgo. A fortiori, it should prefer those whose use beyond a very moderate amount it considers positively harmful. Taxing stimulants up to the point that yields the greatest revenue is consequently not merely permissible but desirable, provided the State needs all the revenue raised.

Whether selling these commodities should be made a more or less exclusive privilege depends on what the restriction is intended to accomplish. Every public gathering place needs police regulation, and these places especially, since offences against society are particularly likely to originate there. It is therefore proper to allow sales, at least for consumption on the premises, only by people whose respectable conduct is known or vouched for. It is proper to regulate opening and closing hours as needed for public supervision, and to withdraw a licence if the keeper's complicity or incompetence repeatedly leads to breaches of the peace, or if the premises become a meeting place for planning and preparing crimes. I do not consider further restrictions justifiable in principle. Limiting the number of beer and spirit-houses expressly to make access harder and reduce temptation, for example, inconveniences everyone because some would abuse ready access. Such a policy also belongs only to a society openly treating the working classes as children or savages, subjected to restrictive education to prepare them for eventual admission to freedom's privileges. No free country professes to govern its working classes on this principle. Anyone who properly values freedom cannot agree to such government unless every effort to educate them for freedom and govern them as free people has been exhausted, and they have conclusively proved governable only as children. The mere statement of this alternative is enough to reveal how absurd it would be to suppose that all those efforts had already been made in any of the cases we need to consider here. Only the mass of contradictions in this country's institutions allows practices belonging to despotic, or so-called paternal, government to enter our system. At the same time, our institutions' general freedom prevents the degree of control needed to make those restraints effective as moral education.

Earlier in this Essay I pointed out that individual liberty in matters concerning only oneself entails a corresponding freedom for any number of people to arrange by mutual agreement matters concerning them jointly and nobody else. There is no difficulty while everyone's wishes remain unchanged. But wishes can change, so even in matters concerning only themselves people often need to enter commitments with one another. Generally, it is right that they keep those commitments. Probably every country's laws, however, recognise exceptions. People are released not only from commitments violating third parties' rights, but sometimes from commitments considered harmful to themselves. In this country and most other civilised countries, for example, an agreement to sell oneself, or let oneself be sold, into slavery would be void. Neither law nor public opinion would enforce it. The reason for limiting someone's voluntary disposal of his own future is especially clear in this extreme case. Respect for liberty is the reason not to interfere with voluntary actions except for others' sake. A voluntary choice shows that what a person chooses is desirable, or at least bearable, to him. His good is generally best secured by allowing him to pursue it in his own way. But selling himself into slavery abandons that liberty and renounces every future exercise of it beyond this one act. He thereby defeats, in his own case, the very purpose that justifies allowing him control over himself. After that sale he is no longer a free person. The condition in which he subsequently lives no longer carries the presumption in its favour that we could draw if he were voluntarily choosing, from day to day, to remain in that condition. Freedom's principle cannot require freedom to cease being free. Being allowed to surrender one's freedom permanently is not freedom. These reasons plainly apply much more widely, although this particular case displays their force especially clearly. Everywhere, however, life's necessities limit their application: life constantly requires us, not to abandon freedom, but to consent to particular restrictions on it. Nevertheless, the principle demanding unrestricted action in purely personal matters requires that people bound to one another in affairs involving no third party should be able to release one another from their agreement. Even without mutual release, perhaps no commitments except those concerning money or money's worth can safely be declared absolutely irrevocable. In the excellent essay already quoted, Baron Wilhelm von Humboldt states his belief that commitments involving personal relations or services should never remain legally binding beyond a limited period. Marriage, the most important such commitment, has the special feature that its purposes fail unless both parties' feelings support it. He therefore holds that either party's declared wish should suffice to dissolve it. This subject is too important and complicated for a passing discussion. I mention it only as far as illustration requires. Had the brevity and general scope of Baron Humboldt's dissertation not obliged him to state his conclusion without discussing its premises, he would surely have acknowledged that the grounds he considers are too simple to settle the question. When someone's explicit promise or conduct encourages another to rely on his continuing to act in a certain way--to form expectations and plans, and stake some part of a life plan on that assumption--new moral obligations towards that person arise. They may be overridden, but cannot be ignored. Moreover, the relationship between two contracting parties may affect other people, placing them in a particular situation or, as in marriage, even bringing them into existence. Both parties then acquire duties towards those third persons. Whether those obligations towards third persons can be fulfilled, or at all events the manner in which they will be fulfilled, must depend very substantially on whether the relationship between the two original parties continues or is broken off. This does not mean, nor can I accept, that those obligations require the agreement's fulfilment at any cost to an unwilling party's happiness. But they are an essential consideration. Even if, as Von Humboldt maintains, they should leave the parties' legal freedom to withdraw unchanged--and I too believe they should make little legal difference--they necessarily make a great difference to moral freedom. Before taking a step affecting such important interests of others, a person must consider all these circumstances. Failure to give their interests proper weight makes him morally responsible for the wrong. I offer these obvious remarks to clarify liberty's general principle, not because this particular question needs them. On the contrary, it is usually discussed as though children's interests were everything and adults' interests nothing.

I have already noted that the absence of recognised general principles causes liberty to be granted where it should be withheld, as well as withheld where it should be granted. In modern Europe, one of the strongest feelings for liberty arises precisely where I think it wholly misplaced. People should be free to act as they please in their own concerns. They should not enjoy the same freedom when acting for others, under the pretence that another person's affairs are their own. While respecting each individual's freedom in matters specially concerning himself, the State must vigilantly supervise whatever power it allows him to exercise over others. This duty is almost entirely neglected within family relations, whose direct effect on human happiness exceeds that of all other relations combined. We need not dwell here on husbands' nearly despotic power over wives. Giving wives the same rights and legal protection as everyone else would wholly remove the evil. Moreover, defenders of established injustice here do not appeal to liberty: they openly champion power. With children, however, mistaken ideas of liberty genuinely obstruct the State's duties. One might almost think a man's children were literally, rather than figuratively, part of himself. Public opinion guards his absolute, exclusive control over them against the slightest legal interference more jealously than it guards him against almost any restriction on his own actions. People generally value power so much more than liberty. Consider education. Is it not almost self-evident that the State should require and enforce a certain standard of education for every human being born its citizen? Yet who is unafraid to acknowledge and assert this truth? Almost everyone admits that parents--or the father, under present law and custom--have one of their most sacred duties, after bringing someone into the world, in educating that person to fulfil his part in life towards others and himself. Although everyone declares this the father's duty, scarcely anyone here can bear the suggestion that he be compelled to perform it. Instead of requiring effort or sacrifice to secure the child's education, we let him decide whether to accept even education supplied free of charge! People still fail to recognise that bringing a child into existence without a reasonable prospect of providing both food for its body and instruction and training for its mind is a moral crime against the unfortunate child and society alike. It is likewise still not recognised that, when the parent fails to fulfil this obligation towards the child, the State ought to see that it is fulfilled, and ought as far as possible to place the expense of doing so upon the parent himself.

Once the duty to enforce universal education was accepted, the present difficulties over what the State should teach and how it should teach would end. These disputes now turn education into a battlefield for sects and parties, wasting in quarrels the time and effort that should educate children. By resolving to require a good education for every child, government could spare itself the task of providing it. Parents could arrange education wherever and however they preferred. The government could simply help poorer children's families pay fees and cover all school expenses for those with nobody else to pay. The objections reasonably urged against State education do not apply to requiring the State to ensure that children are educated. They apply to the State taking upon itself the direction of the education those children receive. Enforcing education and directing it are entirely different undertakings. I object as strongly as anyone to placing all or much of the people's education in State hands. Everything argued here for individuality of character and diversity of opinion and conduct implies the equally inexpressible importance of diverse education. A general State education is simply a means of moulding people into exact likeness. Its mould suits whichever power dominates government: monarch, priesthood, aristocracy, or the majority of the present generation. The more efficiently and successfully it works, the more completely it establishes a despotism over minds, naturally tending towards one over bodies. State-established and State-controlled education, if it exists at all, should be only one among many competing experiments. It should offer an example and stimulus that helps maintain others at a certain standard of excellence. An exception arises if society is so backward that it cannot or will not create proper educational institutions unless government undertakes the task. Government may then, as the lesser of two great evils, run schools and universities, just as it may perform the work of joint stock companies where private enterprise capable of major industrial undertakings does not exist. Generally, however, if enough qualified people exist to provide education under government direction, those same people can and will provide equally good education voluntarily. Compulsory education, combined with State assistance for those unable to pay, would give them the necessary assurance of remuneration.

Public examinations covering all children from an early age would be the necessary means of enforcing this law. A fixed age could be set for examining every child to establish whether he or she can read. If not, the father, unless he has an adequate excuse, could face a moderate fine, payable through labour if necessary, and the child could be sent to school at his expense. The examination should recur annually, with an expanding range of subjects, making the acquisition--and, still more importantly, retention--of a minimum general knowledge effectively compulsory. Above that minimum, voluntary examinations should be available in every subject, with certificates for everyone reaching a specified standard. To prevent the State from using this system to influence opinion improperly, examination requirements, even at advanced levels, should be confined to facts and positive science, apart from instrumental knowledge such as languages and their use. Examinations on religion, politics, and other disputed topics should test not whether opinions are true or false, but the fact that particular authors, schools, or churches hold particular opinions for particular reasons. Regarding disputed truths, the next generation would be no worse off under this system than now. They would still be brought up as churchmen or dissenters, but the State would ensure they became educated churchmen or educated dissenters. Nothing would stop parents choosing religious instruction at the same schools that taught other subjects. Every State attempt to bias citizens' conclusions on disputed questions is wrong. But the State may properly establish and certify that someone has the knowledge needed to make his conclusions on a subject worth hearing. A philosophy student would benefit from being able to pass examinations in both Locke and Kant, whether he follows either or neither. Nor is there any reasonable objection to examining an atheist on Christianity's evidences, provided he need not profess belief in them. Examinations in advanced knowledge should, however, be wholly voluntary. Allowing governments to exclude people from professions, even teaching, for alleged lack of qualifications would give them dangerously excessive power. I agree with Wilhelm von Humboldt that degrees and other public certificates of scientific or professional attainment should be given to everyone who presents himself and passes the examination. But possessing such a certificate should confer no special advantage over a competitor who does not possess one. Its holder should gain only the advantage that public opinion itself chooses to attach to the certificate's testimony about his knowledge or professional attainments.

Education is not the only field where mistaken ideas of liberty prevent recognition of parents' moral obligations and the imposition of legal obligations, although the strongest grounds always exist for the former and often for the latter. Bringing a human being into existence is itself among life's most responsible acts. To assume that responsibility, granting a life that may become a curse or a blessing, without giving the new person at least the ordinary chance of a desirable existence, is a crime against that person. In an overpopulated country, or one threatened with overpopulation, having more than a very small number of children, whose competition reduces labour's reward, is a serious offence against everyone living by the earnings of labour. Laws in many Continental countries forbidding marriage unless the couple can show means to support a family do not exceed the State's legitimate authority. Whether such laws are expedient depends chiefly on local circumstances and feelings, but they cannot be condemned as violations of liberty. They are State interventions to prevent a harmful act, an act injuring others that deserves condemnation and social stigma even where adding legal punishment is considered unwise. Yet current ideas of liberty, which so readily accept genuine intrusions on individual freedom in purely personal matters, resist every attempt to restrain someone's inclinations when satisfying them condemns a child or children to misery and depravity. They resist that restraint even though the resulting harm extends beyond the offspring themselves, bringing many kinds of evil upon everyone sufficiently within their reach to be affected in any way by their subsequent actions. Comparing humanity's strange respect for liberty with its equally strange disrespect, one might imagine an indispensable right to harm others, and no right at all to please oneself without hurting anyone.

I have left until last a broad class of questions about the limits of government intervention. Closely connected with this Essay's subject, they do not strictly belong to it. Here the reasons against intervention do not depend on liberty. The issue is helping individuals, rather than restraining them: should government do something for their benefit, or arrange for it to be done, instead of leaving them to do it themselves, separately or in voluntary association?
Where government intervention does not violate liberty, objections to that intervention may nevertheless arise on three different grounds.

The first is that individuals are likely to perform the task better than government. Generally, those personally interested in a business are best qualified to manage it, or to decide how and by whom it should be managed. This principle condemns the interference in ordinary industrial processes once so commonly practised by legislatures and government officials. Political economists have already discussed this part of the subject sufficiently, however, and it has no particular connection with the principles of this Essay.

The second objection lies closer to our subject. In many cases, individuals may on average perform a particular task less well than government officials. Nevertheless, letting them do it is desirable as a means of educating their minds: strengthening their active faculties, exercising their judgement, and giving them practical familiarity with the matters left in their hands. This is a principal, though not the only, recommendation for jury trials in non-political cases, for free and popular local and municipal institutions, and for voluntary associations managing industrial and philanthropic enterprises. These concern development rather than liberty, with only indirect tendencies connecting them to liberty. A different occasion would be needed to discuss them fully as elements of national education. They are, in truth, the distinctive training of citizens, the practical political education of a free people. They draw people out of the narrow selfishness of personal and family concerns, teaching them to understand shared interests and manage common affairs, to act from public or partly public motives, and to guide themselves by aims that unite rather than separate them. Without these habits and capacities, a free constitution cannot function or survive. The frequently short life of political freedom where adequate local liberties are lacking demonstrates this. Allowing local communities to manage purely local business, and voluntary investors to combine in managing great industrial enterprises, also offers every advantage already described in this Essay of individual development and varied methods of action. Government activity tends towards uniformity everywhere. Individuals and voluntary associations, by contrast, offer varied experiments and an endless diversity of experience. The State can usefully collect the experience of these many trials in a central store and actively circulate and spread it. Its task is to let each experimenter learn from others' experiments, rather than permit only experiments of its own.

The third and strongest reason for limiting government intervention is the great harm of increasing governmental power unnecessarily. Every added function extends the government's influence over people's hopes and fears. It increasingly turns the active and ambitious public into dependants of the government or of a party seeking to become the government. Suppose roads, railways, banks, insurance offices, great joint-stock companies, universities, and public charities were all government branches. Suppose municipal corporations and local boards, with everything they now handle, also became departments of central administration. Suppose everyone employed by these enterprises received appointment and pay from the government and looked to it for every advancement. Neither complete press freedom nor a popularly constituted legislature could then make this or any other country free except in name. The more efficiently and scientifically the administrative machinery was constructed, and the better its arrangements for securing the most capable workers and thinkers, the greater the evil would become. England has recently considered choosing every civil servant through competitive examination, to recruit the most intelligent and educated people available. Much has been said and written on both sides. Opponents especially insist that permanent State employment offers too little income and importance to attract the highest talents, who can always find more inviting careers in the professions, companies, or other public bodies. This argument would not have surprised us coming from supporters, as an answer to the proposal's chief difficulty. Coming from opponents, it is strange. Their objection is actually the proposed system's safety-valve. If all the country's finest talent could indeed be drawn into government service, a proposal helping to achieve that would give genuine cause for alarm. Imagine every activity requiring organised co-operation or broad, comprehensive understanding in government hands, and every government position filled by the ablest people. Apart from purely theoretical thinkers, all the country's broad cultivation and practised intelligence would be concentrated in a large bureaucracy. Everyone else would look to it for everything: the multitude for instructions in every undertaking, the able and aspiring for personal advancement. Entering this bureaucracy and rising within it would become the sole objects of ambition. The public outside it would lack the practical experience needed to criticise or restrain its methods. Even if the accidents of despotism or the normal working of popular institutions occasionally brought reforming rulers to power, no reform contrary to bureaucratic interests could be achieved. Accounts by adequately informed observers describe this as the Russian empire's unhappy condition. The Czar himself cannot overcome the bureaucratic body. He can send any individual official to Siberia, but cannot govern without the officials or against their will. Over every decree he issues they exercise a tacit power of veto. They need not openly oppose his command: merely refraining from putting it into effect is enough to make the command powerless. In more civilised countries with a stronger spirit of rebellion, people expect the State to do everything for them, or at least undertake nothing themselves without asking it for permission and even instructions. They naturally blame it for every misfortune. When suffering exceeds their patience, they rise against the government and make what is called a revolution. Someone else then jumps into the seat of power, with or without legitimate authority from the nation, and gives orders to the bureaucracy. After that change at the top, the conduct of affairs continues very much as it did before. The bureaucratic body itself has not changed, and there is nobody outside it with the capacity to take its place and carry on its work.

A people accustomed to managing its own affairs presents a very different picture. In France, so many people have served in the military, often at least as non-commissioned officers, that every popular uprising contains several people able to lead and improvise a workable plan. Americans possess the same ability in every kind of civil business that the French possess in military affairs. Leave a group of Americans without government, and they can improvise one, conducting it or any other public business with adequate intelligence, order, and resolution. Every free people ought to have this character. A people that does is certain to remain free: it will never submit to enslavement by a person or group merely because they can seize and operate the central administration. No bureaucracy could hope to make such people do or endure anything they reject. Where everything operates through bureaucracy, however, nothing it seriously opposes can be accomplished. Such countries organise their national experience and practical ability into a disciplined body to govern everyone else. The more perfect this organisation becomes, and the more successfully it recruits and trains the most capable people from every social rank, the more complete everyone's bondage becomes, including that of the bureaucrats themselves. The governors are as enslaved to their organisation and discipline as the governed are to their governors. A Chinese mandarin is as much despotism's creature and instrument as the humblest cultivator. An individual Jesuit is his order's slave to the utmost point of degradation, although the order itself exists to secure its members' collective power and importance.

We must also remember that drawing all a country's leading ability into its governing body eventually destroys that body's own intellectual activity and capacity for progress. United in operating a system that, like every system, necessarily follows fixed rules to a considerable extent, officials are constantly tempted to lapse into idle routine. If they occasionally leave that horse-mill circuit, they may rush into some crude, half-examined scheme that has caught a leading member's fancy. These seemingly opposite but closely related tendencies have only one check. Only exposure to vigilant criticism from equally able people outside the official body can stimulate it to maintain a high intellectual standard. Means must therefore exist independently of government to develop such ability and provide the opportunities and experience required for sound judgement in great practical affairs. If we want permanently skilful and efficient officials--above all, officials able to devise improvements and willing to adopt them--their body must not monopolise every occupation that develops and cultivates the faculties needed to govern human beings. Otherwise our bureaucracy will decline into a pedantocracy.

At what point do these formidable evils for human freedom and progress begin? More precisely, when do they outweigh the benefits of society applying its combined strength, under recognised leaders, to remove obstacles to its well-being? How can we gain the greatest advantages of centralised power and intelligence without directing too much of society's general activity into governmental channels? These are among the most difficult and complicated questions in governing. Much depends on details. Numerous different considerations must be kept in view, and no absolute rule is possible. Nevertheless, I believe a practical principle of safety can be stated, an ideal to guide us and a standard against which to test proposed arrangements: spread power as widely as efficiency permits, while centralising information as fully as possible and distributing it from that centre. In municipal administration, for example, as in the New England States, every task not better left to those directly concerned would be divided in minute detail among separate, locally elected officers. Alongside this, each branch of local affairs would have central supervision forming part of the general government. That supervisory body would bring together the varied information and experience gained from managing the same public business in every locality, from comparable work abroad, and from the general principles of political science. It should have the right to know everything done, and a special duty to make knowledge gained in one place available elsewhere. Its higher position and broad field of observation would free it from a locality's petty prejudices and narrow outlook, giving its advice natural authority. But as a permanent institution, its actual power should, I believe, extend only to compelling local officers to follow the laws governing them. In matters not covered by general rules, those officers should exercise their own judgement, answerable to their constituents. For breaking rules they should answer to the law, and the legislature should establish the rules themselves. Central administration should merely supervise their execution. Where they are not properly carried out, it should turn, according to the case, either to the courts to enforce the law or to the electorate to remove officials who have failed to execute its spirit. Broadly, this is the intended central supervision of the Poor Law Board over administrators of the Poor Rate throughout the country. The Board's additional powers were right and necessary in that special case, to cure entrenched mismanagement in affairs deeply affecting the whole community, not merely particular localities. No locality has a moral right to turn itself through mismanagement into a nest of pauperism, inevitably overflowing into neighbouring districts and damaging the entire working population's moral and physical condition. The Poor Law Board's powers of administrative coercion and subordinate legislation, though exercised very sparingly because of prevailing opinion, are fully justified in a matter of the highest national importance. They would be entirely misplaced in supervising purely local interests. But a central body supplying information and instruction to every locality would be equally valuable throughout administration. Government cannot do too much of the work that helps and stimulates individual effort and development without obstructing them. Harm begins when it replaces the activity of individuals and groups with its own rather than calling forth their powers; when, instead of informing, advising, and sometimes condemning, it makes them work in chains or tells them to stand aside while it works for them. In the long run, a State's worth is the worth of its individual members. A State that subordinates their intellectual growth and elevation to a little more administrative skill--or the appearance of skill produced by routine practice in details--diminishes its people to make them more obedient instruments, even for beneficial purposes. It will discover that small people cannot truly accomplish great things. The perfect machinery for which it sacrificed everything will ultimately achieve nothing, because it has banished the vital force needed to animate it merely to make that machinery run more smoothly.
